speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, the governor of the Bank of Canada said in his annual report what we have been saying in this House for some time that weekly wages are falling behind consumer prices. He said:
__it does not seem realistic to expect them to accept-other than very briefly

Oral Questions
in view of the fact that wages in the past year as a result of the AIB controls have fallen behind consumer prices, on a composite index, at an annual rate of approximately $666, I ask the minister what the policy of the government is, in the absence of any guidelines with respect to wage earners whose incomes are falling behind consumer prices.

subsubtopic: DISPARITY BETWEEN WAGE INCREASES AND CONSUMER PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I presented my budget in November, I said that the rate of inflation would go down in 1979. In fact, the predictions are still to the effect that the rate of inflation for this year will be lower than last year. I think that the present rate of inflation, while a bit high, will go down during the year.
Labour and management will be well advised to make sure that there is not a new round of large wage increases which will lead to big price increases, which will put us back into the position we were at in 1974. I think that Canadian workers and managers understand that. They realize that we have regained, through moderation, our competitive position in world markets. That is why, for example, in the last quarter of 1978 we had a Canadian utilization of manufacturing capacity of close to 90 per cent. We have seen a big increase in employment in Canada. That is because Canadians are willing to be responsible in order to have a better economy.

subsubtopic: DISPARITY BETWEEN WAGE INCREASES AND CONSUMER PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Perhaps I can ask the minister if he agrees with the statement of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I ask him to address himself to that, especially in light of forecasts for the current year. In light of these very alarming statistics, and the fact that wage earners in this country have been held down while prices have been allowed to escalate, does the minister agree with this statement by the governor of the Bank of Canada? If so, what does he intend to do about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED AIR CANADA BARGAIN RATE FLIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the course of action is very much in the hands of the United States, so I can only report where they stand in relation to their power to suspend or not suspend certain tariffs which have been filed by Canadian air carriers.
As I understand the American position at this moment, they did register a conditional note in relation to the fares filed by Air Canada, but they do not want these to take effect at this stage. Therefore, as I read the situation, the early part of the Air Canada lower fare season will certainly come into effect without impediment if the Americans do not change their position and take different action. At the same time, they have reserved the right to observe what happens to fares which may be filed by American carriers. Hon. members will know that the Canadian Transport Commission has been allowing certain of these fares similar to the Air Canada fares to come into effect when filed by carriers from the United States.

The American note also indicated that they would await the outcome of the discussions between Canada and the United States before taking any further action. Since those discussions are due to start in several weeks, it seems obvious that the first several weeks of the Air Canada program will be all right. Whether the rest of the program will be all right, obviously will depend on the conclusion of those discussions. I have no reason to doubt that they will be all right.

I think we requested those discussions last September or November, but only now have the Americans agreed to having them and they will be held in April.
In the course of looking at the Air Canada fares, the Canadian Transport Commission indicated that certain parallel and similar fares filed by air carries from the United States would indeed be allowed. In other words, they would no longer be suspended and, therefore, they can go into effect. As I listened to the statement made by the government House leader, I did not hear him include the suggestion that has been made, namely that at second reading there be only one speaker per party and that speeches be limited to 20 minutes. It seems to me that that ought to be included in the order or in the understanding.
It is also a fact that in the letter which the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) wrote to the government House leader, there was a suggestion that, if necessary, there would be a readiness to cancel private members' hour. This matter might not take all day, but if we have the understanding that having gone into this matter today we not have a private members' hour from five o'clock until six o'clock, it would help us deal with this matter satisfactorily. At any rate, what I am saying is: yes, we agree.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to explain very clearly my party's position in relation to this issue. As the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada in the House, I think I have always contributed very positively to the proper consideration of the bills which are introduced in the House to enable all hon. members to express their views. A few moments ago I heard the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) talk about the road to Damascus. Mr. Speaker, I for one am not a convert to this position.
I agree about the activities which are necessary if the House of Commons is to administer our country properly. I have said it and repeated it and I will repeat it again. There are 264 of us here, mandated by Canadians to administer the business of the country. Mr. Speaker, if I cannot express my views, I will forget all about it. But if you allow me to express them, I would like to explain very openly to my hon. colleagues of the House the way we see things and say that we are willing to work to allow parliament to be truly effective. As the President of the Privy Council said, we have before us Bill C-49 dealing with banks. The purpose of the bill is to extend the present Bank Act. I for one am not ready to allow it to pass without saying what I think about it. That is also true of my colleagues. This is the third time such a thing happens. We will have to come to a conclusion about all this.
Moreover, Bill C-32 on boycotts is another important bill which should not be passed hastily, but rather considered very seriously so that parliament and then the government can implement it. The bill should be efficient. We also have before us, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-38 on the excise tax. This is a very important bill, Mr. Speaker. I think we should take time to study it seriously and make the necessary amendments so that the legislation which will be part of our statutes is efficient. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am ready as are my colleagues to accept to limit the time we deal with this bill. I agree with that but I want leaders of the House to come to an arrangement; I do not want us to be taken by surprise or on short notice.
I would like the President of the Privy Council to take into consideration the remarks I am making now. I think however that we, not me but others, are bright enough to come to an
Business of the House
honest and serious settlement and that Tuesday could be a day allotted to the opposition, as the Leader of the Opposition announced. I understood he said yes. I understood March 26 would be an opposition day and I am quite willing to accept that on behalf of my colleagues but I would like parliament to be expeditious. Not that I want to have innocent parliamentarians ready to accept anything whatever the conditions may be. I would like the people of my country to get the impression that we are responsible, that we take enough time to study such and such bill but not too much; I would like that we come to a practical conclusion so that the administration of my country be the best of all democratic countries on this human earth.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-469, to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 (admission of entrepreneur trainees).

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMISSION OF ENTREPRENEUR TRAINEES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMISSION OF ENTREPRENEUR TRAINEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill fills an important gap in Canada's immigration policy. Immigrants who have come to Canada and established successful businesses and are ready to expand often feel they will be best served by bringing relatives from their own country to help their business to grow. They have more confidence in, and a better relationship with, relatives. Such arrivals do not take existing jobs from Canadians but in fact may add new jobs. My bill will establish a new category of immigrants, entrepreneur trainees, who come to Canada and will eventually earn landed immigrant status.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASED PENALTY FOR AIR CHARTER TOUR OVERBOOKING
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-470, respecting inclusive air charters.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASED PENALTY FOR AIR CHARTER TOUR OVERBOOKING
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASED PENALTY FOR AIR CHARTER TOUR OVERBOOKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to discourage operators of inclusive air charter tours from overbooking or otherwise failing to provide the accommodation that is advertised as part of the tour. At present, a tour operator has nothing to lose by gambling, for instance, on the number of hotel rooms available at a destination. The customer is only reimbursed for the value of what he does not receive, not for any inconvenience that results from being stranded. The bill would impose a penalty of three times the value of any part of the tour omitted, payable to the customer.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I was going to rise yesterday but something happened during the course of points of order and I was not able to draw this to the attention of the parliamentary secretary. I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Young) answering today. I am hopeful that I will have more success with him in getting responses to my legitimate, important and urgent questions on the order paper.
The fact simply is this. I have to persist in bringing this matter to the attention of the parliamentry secretary in order to get a response to these important questions. I refer to questions I placed on the order paper with regard to the use of government aircraft by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of the cabinet during the two-month period prior to the byelection. The parliamentary secretary will know that I am referring to questions Nos. 207 and 208 which read as follows:
Has the Liberal Party of Canada paid for the use of any government aircraft in the period August 16 to October 16, 1978, in connection with the byelections held on October 16, 1978 and, if so, in what amount for each trip?

Did the Prime Minister or Members of the Cabinet, during the period August 16 to October 16, 1978, make use of government aircraft and, if so, what was the total cost and what was the destination, on each occasion?
I keep raising this matter because as each day goes by we get closer and closer to a general election. The problem is this. If the government persists in not answering these questions before the general election, there can be only one conclusion: the government would be embarrassed by revealing that information. In the interests of protection whatever remains of the reputation of this government, I ask the parliamentary secretary to try and get the answers to those questions and to others that I have placed on the order paper.

subtopic: DELAY IN ANSWERING ORDER PAPER QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with regard to questions I have had on the order paper for three sessions. A period of two or three years has elapsed and there has been no attempt to give me any type of answer even though individuals from the department have contacted my office for clarification of some of the questions I asked.
I wish to underscore what the previous member stated to this chamber. It is obvious the government is very touchy when it comes to questions about passes for travelling, not only when they relate to members of the cabinet but also when they affect presidents of Crown corporations and commissioners. My purpose was to find out how often persons in these positions have travelled on special passes issued to them. I reinforce the appeal made to the parliamentary secretary by the hon. member in the hope of having these questions answered before an election.

speechtext:
that Bill C-49, to amend the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Banks Act, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill I am now introducing is short and very straightforward. The purpose of it is to extend the powers of banks incorporated under the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Banks Act to April 1, 1980, by amending section 6 of those pieces of legislation. Under the present legislation, Mr. Speaker, the powers of banks to operate as banks would expire on March 31, 1979.

Bill C-15, the Banks and Banking Law Revision Act, has been under consideration by committees of the Senate and the House since November of last year, although the bill was presented in the same form to the House of Commons in June, 1978. An extension of the present Bank Act is necessary because there is not sufficient time between now and March 31 to permit a careful examination of the committees' reports, and to consider any changes that should be made to the proposals in Bill C-15 in response to the committees' recommendations.
I share the disappointment of various members of the House and of the many interested parties who have indicated their desire to have the revised banking legislation enacted as soon as possible. However, I do feel that the decennial revision of the banking legislation should not be carried out without careful review and extensive consultation.
The parliamentary committees have devoted a great deal of their time to examining this important and extremely complex legislation. Interested parties have had every opportunity to submit written briefs and to be heard by the committees. The entire revision process, which began in September, 1974, when the then minister of finance invited interested parties to submit briefs on the subject, has been time consuming but most worth-while. While it has become evident that revised banking legislation cannot be enacted before March 31, 1979, I would hope that it will be passed as soon as possible thereafter.

subtopic: BANK ACT AND QUEBEC SAVINGS BANKS ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was touch and go whether we would go on with this bill today.
I was anticipating that in the present circumstances we might either go on with the boycott bill or with the bill which has already been started, Bill C-38, the exicse tax bill, which is a matter of much greater interest to most members of the House. However, Bill C-49 is before us and, as far as I am concerned, I hope we will stick to its provisions which call for an extension of one year of the Bank Act.
I should like to go into a little more detail, though, with regard to what has happened and why we find ourselves in our present situation; I believe this could be instructive not only to ourselves but to all concerned. What does one do when the House has to consider a decennial revision of the Bank Act in the context of significant changes and developments affecting the economy and industrial activity in this country? I took part in the previous revision of the Bank Act which began in 1964 and finished in 1967. For that reason I feel no compunction of conscience should the study of these revisions provoke any adverse comment from anyone except those who think that, having once proposed something, it should be considered for five minutes and then accepted.
I recall that back in 1972-73, as finance critic for the opposition I recommended to the then minister of finance, Mr. John Turner, that he should convince his cabinet colleagues to appoint a royal commission on the subject of banking and financial institutions in this country. The Porter commission, which was appointed in 1959 or 1960, reported about 1964. That commission did very good work.
We are not legislating now for the past but for the decade to come-the coming two decades as far as our banking system is concerned. The subject matter we reviewed in the sixties and that w' ich we are reviewing in the seventies are as different as chalk trom cheese where banking and related matters are concerned. The evolution of business activities, business techniques and so forth has been such that we are no longer in the same field. There was always a constant danger of limiting one's thinking to what had gone past. I accused the committee several times of legislating back to the use of quill pens or for the manufacture of horses' collars when everybody is using automobiles.
As a result of strong representations made in the committee by myself and others, a general consensus was reached that we would legislate for the present and for the future. However, we did not have the material, studies and testimony from all sides we would have required. Therefore, I fault my old friend John

March 22, 1979
Bank Act
Turner for not setting up that royal commission so that we could have the benefit of a good report, which might have taken three years to present. It would have served the committee in the other House as well as ours. Incidentally, the committees finished their studies approximately three or four days apart.
There was a great deal of consensus among the members who attended, members of the official opposition and the government party. Rarely did we see members of the New Democratic Party; I do not think they attended more than four or five sessions. Possibly they attended a few at which witnesses appeared, but beyond that and with respect to the preparation of the report we did not see them. We did not see others very much either. On the other hand, people did get to know the subject. The committee considered Bill C-57 last June and set a schedule for testimony during the fall months. That schedule was interrupted. I think the parliamentary secretary will agree that it was interrupted because the government decided to put the session to an end and start a new session.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) will agree that the committee did lose about a month of momentum as a result of that. That was a consequence of a government decision. Perhaps that decision was made for valid reasons, but that was one of the consequences. We did hear all the witnesses. The committee split into subcommittees to hear testimony. Questioning was full and we received a good reaction from the public.
As far as the recommendations of the committee were concerned, the report took a little longer, I think because members decided to be extraordinarily careful. Some sixty recommendations were made. I will not go into the subject matter of the recommendations; I think that would be irrelevant.
The question now is why we are extending the Bank Act for one year. There will be some rather difficult consequences. There will be competition from foreign banks and uncertainty on the part of Caisses Populaires. There will be delay in the setting up of the proposed Canada payments association. There will be some difficulty with regard to some Caisses Populaires and credit unions. There will be other uncertainties which have not been resolved. The Senate report and the report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs each have about 60 recommendations, in addition to which some time before Christmas the government presented some 70 technical amendments.
Some of them were not so technical, but the bill has to go back to square one, and even if the committees had reported in mid-February there was no way the government could have considered the two reports. I do not think the Minister of Finance has a closed mind on this subject, but whichever government carries out the redrafting of the Bank Act will have to consider the recommendations of the committee of the other House and ours on the subject, what the act should

contain and particularly certain definitions which will have some rather far-reaching consequences. All this will entail some deep rethinking. Once the thinking has been completed there will have to be legal drafting and translation. Then there will be the introduction of a bill and debate at second reading, which there has not been in this House.
If there were to be a second reading debate on a bank bill in this House, I am sure it would be long and wide-ranging because every member of this House feels that he is the most inspired critic of the banking system, depending, of course, on when he had his last conversation with his favourite bank manager about the size of his overdraft. Then there would have to be consideration in committee. That consideration would not necessarily entail public hearings, but there were public hearings with respect to the previous proposed revision.
The Canadian Bankers' Association represents those organizations most affected, and it made appearances. I think perhaps there were some others, but the list was much smaller than on previous occasions. After the committee stage there would be a report stage. The previous bill was some 360 pages long and affected five different acts. In fact, it set up one new act, the proposed Canadian payments association act.
There would have been no way within six weeks of sitting time, even if we had dedicated all our sitting time to consideration of the Bank Act, that we would have concluded our business in time, passed the bill at third reading, had it go to the other place for consideration and had it in place in time for the banks to take the necessary positions so that as of April 1 they could have carried on business. That was just not in the cards, and in this regard I am glad to see that the government has not chosen, for example, October 1 next, but instead April 1, 1980. I think that is a realistic date under any circumstances because consideration of the Bank Act will have to fit in with many other matters which have to come before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Once being seized of a matter a committee cannot set it aside or have part of its membership consider other matters.
I had to laugh at the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mac-Eachen) today when he alleged that the opposition House leader reeled under the shock of his observations. The man who is most responsible for the horse and buggy pace of this House with regard to legislation is the present Deputy Prime Minister. Since 1976 he has consistently refused to refer certain matters of procedure which Mr. Speaker has indicated should be considered and on which there has been general agreement on both sides of the House that they should be put into practice at least for a trial period to see how they work. However, unless and until we get rid of the self-inflicted hair shirt constructed by the predecessor of the Minister of Finance when he was government House leader back in 1969 that standing committees consider legislation and estimates at the same time, there will be no way to consider legislation other than to go from the House to the standing committees.
March 22, 1979

The finance comm'ttee has its plate way overloaded, what with the estimates from five departments and, usually, not the majority share but a very large proportion of the legislation that comes before this chamber. Surely to goodness we have several options open to us to change the procedure whereby committees could be freed of the entanglements of a number of representations.
I will not go into the whole picture, but suffice it to say that we are working under a system that was thought to be copied from the British back in the 1960s. They carried it for a short while and then tossed it into the can because it was not worth it, and now they are well away from it. The same with this particular bill. I hope that if in due course we have to do this again, if we have to do it with other pieces of legislation that have sunset clauses or make a major impact in the House, we will have special legislative committees to deal with them. Members can move from committee to committee, but committees cannot move from committee to committee, nor can you shift legislation from committee to committee if there is an overloading.
All right, we have reached this point and the question is: Is it to be recommended to the House that the Quebec Savings Banks Act be extended to March 31, 1980? In my view it is and it always was. Even when I participated with the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance in setting the date of March 31, 1979, I was told that I did not think it was being realistic. I admit that, like everyone else, I was expecting an election in the interval. We set this date over a year ago and I expected there would be an election but that we would take care of the situation by an extension of the bill in the interval. The events overtook the calendar.
I am not going to fault the present minister. I will say there were two reasons. First of all, I think the former minister, Mr. Turner, was unwise, or it was unfortunate that he was unsuccessful if he tried to convince his colleagues to set up a royal commission on banking. Second, I would fault the minister's predecessor, Mr. Macdonald, the former member for Rose-dale, in that he refused in 1976 or the beginning of 1977 to refer the contents of the green paper to the committee on some imagined ground that there would be a possibility of two debates. I am sure there would not have been. It would have shortened the debate and we would have cleared away a lot of the underbrush; and who knows, at this time we might already have had a new Bank Act on the way to being implemented, one that is in position for the banks to carry on. It seems to me it is as clear as that.
I will not hassle any particular person while using the benefits of 20-20 hindsight, but I am going to say that my colleagues on the finance committee worked endlessly from Monday nights all the way through to Friday mornings sitting three and four sessions a day on Tuesday and Thursday and Wednesday afternoons, in order to accommodate the testimony of the interested public, and particularly to consider the massive material and to formulate the recommendations they have made.
Bank Act
I was glad to co-operate with them and to work with them, and I know the same may be said of the other place. You develop a sort of kinship and the satisfaction of working with your colleagues on both sides of the House to achieve a document which was unanimous in so far as those persons present and voting for its acceptance were concerned. It was a genuine effort at consensus.
I will say this: We are not going to claim that we are the greatest geniuses in the world-some of our provisions can be criticized by any number of people, depending upon their vested interests and their particular viewpoint-but, on the other hand, considering it from here, within our time limitation I think we can be justifiably proud of the work done by many of our colleagues, those who were there regularly as well as those who came sporadically to fill in and to make special contributions when they were particularly interested; and the same may be said of those on the government side.
Similarly, we worked well over a year on the revision of the Income Tax Act. Members develop, I think, the quality that is required by intelligent individuals who are out to achieve a certain purpose in trying to put forward the best possible package for their colleagues to consider. This we hope we have done and we commend it to the government.
I do not want to go into any particular phase of the bill and I hope no one else will. At present the question is simply: Do we extend the Bank Act until March 31, 1980? To me that is the pertinent subject. I hope we can do that and I am ready to go on to Bill C-38.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said that the pertinent subject was whether or not we would extend the Bank Act for another year, he managed to spend considerable time talking about a number of other subjects, which he had every right to do because they related to the question of what is going on at the moment in the finance committee and the recommendations that have been made by that committee to the government on the Bank Act.
I want to indicate to the minister that we will not give him any trouble with the extension of the Bank Act, because we realize that the revisions to the Bank Act which have been recommended by the committee, and to which we in our party have taken exception and filed a minority report, will not, of course, be discussed in the short life which is left to this parliament. If I may say so, the shorter the life, the better, so far as we are concerned.
Be that as it may, I want to make some comments with respect to the recommendations of the committee on the Bank Act, to put on the record what are our objections to those recommendations and what are our concerns with respect to the policies of the government and the policies that have been recommended by the committee.
There are three principal objections that we have to the recommendations that have come forward from the committee. The first objection we have is that we do not agree with and do

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with great respect, I hope Your Honour will allow me exactly the same latitude allowed the hon. member for Edmonton West.
Our third concern respecting the policy in the Bank Act is that we are concerned banks should be seen as instruments of public policy. As such they should be required to make full disclosure and have limitations placed on their profits.
It seems to me these concerns are great. I do not want to take a lot of time debating them or their merits. I want simply to indicate to the government that it would not be possible to bring the Bank Act before parliament without my party exercising, by every means at its disposal, its opposition to those three principles.
We should have a democratic Bank Act, one concerned with the role of banks in the entire economic picture of the country. It should be concerned with guaranteeing the rights and controls of parliament. It should be concerned with the need for full disclosure of information, particularly in the area of foreign loans and loans to countries which are not democratic and are imposing great hardship on their citizens. These matters should be incorporated into the Bank Act. Also we are concerned deeply that the whole question of bank profits should be discussed and considered by the government. We know the limit on interest rates was abandoned in 1967, but since that time I suggest profits have gone too far.
When the government wants to get a piece of legislation through, for example Bill C-14, the unemployment insurance bill, it does not have a great deal of trouble marshalling the votes needed in committee. It is highly ironic. The government did not consult with anyone. It did not consult a number of witnesses. It did not have separate unions, each making a deputation to the committee and going through in great detail what their concerns were.
The government went through that report very quickly, but when it comes to legislation such as the Bank Act, the borrowers and depositors protection act or the competition bill, the government has failed to act. It should have brought in legislation in 1974 or earlier to deal with the problem of competition. It should have brought in legislation and stuck with it to provide information and protection to borrowers and depositors, the people taking out mortgages and loans. It should have provided protection and information on being able to pay off loans and mortgages early without paying an extra
[Mi. Rae.)
sum or penalty fee to the banks or trust companies in question. That type of legislation for the protection of Canadian consumers admittedly would have cost the banks and financial institutions some money and trouble. A competition bill would not have been to the liking of our large corporations because it would have broken some of them up and forced them to compete with each other, something they are not used to. But that type of legislation does not get the attention of the government. It does not get the drive and determination of the government. It does not get the determination of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
The government is prepared to listen to objections, concerns, deputations, and to be lobbied, compromised, whittled away and whittled down so that there is no competition bill before the House at the present time. Also there is no borrowers and depositors protection act or a democratic bank act at the present time. When the government wants to get legislation through which affects the little people in the country, it can do it as quickly as it wants and it does it as quickly as it wants. It imposes closure and everything else. But when it comes to matters affecting the financial institutions, the government dawdles, delays and meanders its way through the legislation, and there is no clear indication of its public policy and determination.
The government is making a major mistake. It has allowed itself to avoid some very important political and economic questions and decisions which would work to the advantage of Canadian consumers. We are concerned about the Bank Act currently before the committee. We have a minority report which the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man) filed. It is before the House and the press. The government knows our concerns. I do not think our concerns are limited to my party; I am sure they are the concerns of others.
There is not a consensus in the country to allow foreign banks to take over. Certainly there is not a consensus to allow banks to withhold critical information and not be subject to profit controls, particularly when it is known that their profits last year were $1 billion. A good deal of the reason for the massive increase in profits simply is the spread banks have been allowed to charge their customers, the difference they have been allowed to collect between the Bank of Canada rate and the rate they are charging their customers. Something should be done about that. Something should be done about the question of foreign ownership in Canada. The method proposed by the government will have the opposite effect.
Returning to Bill C-49, we are not opposed to the extension. If anything, we would like to see a longer extension because of the discussions which might be necessary to get the government to change its mind. We are concerned on behalf of the consumer about the lack of legislation in the financial field. We do not think the consumer has enough information or protection when he goes to a bank or trust company. We do not think there is enough competition in the Canadian marketplace to give the consumer the sovereignty he deserves. The government has had five years to act, but it has not produced the type of legislation which will protect consumers. Now it
March 22, 1979

comes to us and says that it needs another year to revise the Bank Act. The government has a lot to learn. The economic questions, the questions facing Canadian consumers, are most important ones. It is time for the government to come home, to look at these problems and give them the attention and the commitment that they require.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said this afternoon during the debate on the business of the House, I do not want to delay unduly consideration of the various bills that the government wishes to put forward in this place. However, Bill C-49 which is now before us is the exact replica of other measures requesting the extension of the Bank Act for another year which were presented to us in 1977. I remember there was a debate at that time. Finally, the bill was adopted and the Bank Act was extended for a year.
In 1978, the government introduced another measure, Bill C-16, to extend the act for a specific period through clause 1(6) which reads:
(a) if parliament sits on at least twenty days during the month of March, 1979,-
We are now in March, 1979-
-the bank may carry on the business of banking until the first day of April, 1979, and no longer;
Subsection (b) reads as follows:
If parliament does not sit on at least twenty days during the month of March, 1979, the bank may carry on the business of banking until the sixtieth sitting day of parliament next thereafter, and no longer.
Mr. Speaker, I imagine that with Bill C-49 the government is giving notice to the House that parliament will sit on at least twenty days during the month of March, 1979, and that, consequently, it must introduce a bill to extend the Bank Act in our country. Mr. Speaker, the content of Bill C-49 is strangely similar to that of Bill C-16 which the House passed in 1978. It contains exactly the same provisions, which means that the chartered banks could keep operating whether parliament is dissolved or not.
Mr. Speaker, it will come as a surprise to no one that the member for Bellechasse objects to the powers chartered banks are given to translate into money the nation's credit. I find it extraordinary that we should have on top of the public monetary system, a parallel monetary system. If this sort of thing can go on, it is simply because Canadians are not aware of the way our monetary system operates in Canada, which is not surprising.
About a week ago, I met a brave 59-year old public servant who works at Statistics Canada and has always dealt with figures. I will not name him, even if I remember his name, but he told me this: How is it that, at 59 years of age, I still do not know exactly the nature and the operation of our monetary
Bank Act
system, why the dollar exists? He is not the only one, Mr. Speaker. A great many Canadians get up in the morning to go to work and earn dollars. They do not ask themselves, during the day, who created the dollar. But still it was created somewhere, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian dollar had its origin neither in heaven nor in hell; it was created somewhere and it is important to understand its role. Some hon. members, who may have nothing better to say, will think and say, in jest: "Ah! those social crediters always think and talk in terms of dollars".
Mr. Speaker, at my age, with all the years I have behind me, 1 can prove that as a Canadian citizen I have not worked only for money. The large family that I gave to my country, the acres of land that I cleared for cultivation so they would produce to feed the population of my country clearly show that for my part I did not work only for money. I must however admit that the monetary system of my country has a role to play, and this system, and this is a great matter of concern for me, should be under the sole jurisdiction of our government through its institutions. I have never accepted, Mr. Speaker, and I do not accept today that the credit of our country should be controlled by private institutions for their own benefit and that we, Canadians, should be left to fare as best we can by borrowing right and left at excessive interest rates. We are burdening our children with many years of debt to pay for the services that we need today when they will themselves have to pay for other services in 30, 40 or 50 years.
Where are we going, Mr. Speaker? The Canadian parliament must ask this question. I shall try to answer it, and if I am wrong, since we are 264 members of parliament, there will certainly be someone intelligent enough among the 263 others to show me why I am wrong. Mr. Speaker, the credit of the nation is created by someone. First of all, what does the word credit mean? This is important. Before laughing at those who use this word, we should first try to understand what is the real credit of the nation. Who creates it? Mr. Speaker, to my mind, the word credit comes from a latin word which means "I believe, I have confidence".
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I have confidence that a sufficient number of my fellow citizens are able through their work and their intelligence to produce the things I need for myself and my dependants. Their credit means that there is a large enough number of my fellow citizens able to produce the essential services that I and my dependants need, whether they are my wife, my children or others. I have confidence that our activities in general can produce the services required to meet my daily needs. Mr. Speaker, to my mind, this is what credit really means.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if that true credit is made up of our daily activities why could the government not have an institution capable of monetizing credit, making it tangible with dollars, so we can exchange those services and those things among ourselves? Why do we have to go and beg a private

March 22, 1979
Bank Act
institution legally incorporated under a law of this parliament, the chartered banks legislation, allowing us under section 72 to monetize the credit of this country?
The rest of the Bank Act I do not quarrel with. Mr. Speaker, banks operate very smoothly. They keep exemplary accounting. They have extraordinary employees. Indeed, I have a son-in-law who is the manager of a branch in one of our banks and is doing a great job. He earns his living like everyone else and I am proud of him. I never discuss his work, Mr. Speaker. As far as the present legislation is concerned, he is like everyone else working, he is part of the system. It is not people that I quarrel with. It is the system. Mr. Speaker, it is with the discretionary power the chartered banks of this country are given. What does section 72 say? I would like all Canadians to remember that extraordinary power. I will quote so as not to make any mistake: cash and secondary reserves. It means the law determines that banks have to keep in cash and secondary reserves at the Bank of Canada a quantity of bank notes as safeguard. Section 72(1) says:
The bank shall maintain a cash reserve in the form of notes of, and deposits in Canadian currency with, the Bank of Canada, and such reserve shall be not less on the average during any month than an amount equal to
(a)	twelve per cent of such of its deposit liabilities as are payable on demand
in Canadian currency; and
(b)	four per cent of such of its deposit liabilities as are payable after notice in
Canadian currency.
Mr. Speaker, that is the law as it stands. The purpose of Bill C-49 is to determine whether we are going to continue to maintain that discretionary power to create money. It does not matter if it is just figures in a deposit account with chequing privileges.
This week with my colleagues I met young people from the Canadian Forum, students from all parts of the country. I was invited, like my colleagues, to make a speech before them. I was invited to tell them if I really believe that the Parliament of Canada controls the administration of our country. Honestly, I had to tell them that, unfortunately, the Parliament of Canada does not control the administration of my country because of the fact that, as we know, there are three official powers under our constitution, but there is also another power, a super power that is not our constitution but that transcends the three powers that I shall enumerate. First, the legislative power, we the 264 elected representatives assembled in this House. We are here to legislate, to pass laws that will guide our action, the action of Canadians throughout the country and our day to day activities so that we shall respect each other and not be deprived of our rights by the abuses of others. This is what is called the legislative power.
To implement the measures passed by the legislative power, an executive power is obviously needed. We cannot all be part of it. So the executive includes the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien),

one of the senior ministers, who is particularly responsible for matters directly concerning our pocketbooks and this is why we call him Minister of Finance. And there are other ministers, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott), responsible for the implementation of legislation and for taking in our pocketbooks the money needed to implement the laws passed by the Parliament of Canada. He is responsible for the implementation of those laws at the national revenue level. His name is not important. Then the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) responsible for the implementation of laws passed by this parliament to allow each Canadian to benefit from social legislation, old age security and welfare in co-operation with the provinces. This is why it is called the executive. There is also the judiciary responsible for ensuring a standard of justice in the administration of laws. And if an individual, if a Canadian considers that his rights have been infringed upon he is entitled to go before the courts and, until now, I have confidence in the integrity of our courts and the administration of justice.
There might sometimes be offences about which no truly proper decision can be made because there is no evidence. It is also human that there might be decisions which are not entirely faultless. It is not for me to mention particular cases, Mr. Speaker, but I must say that I have confidence in the judiciary, and I consider it my duty to say so. But on top of all that, something which is not provided for in the constitution, there is a super power that I call the monetary super power, and that super power does not care about our constitution, it does not care about anything we might say in this House, because it is completely above any legislation we might adopt, it does not care about the constitution and what we might think, just as a bandit does not care about the law.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I say that Bill C-49 to extend the Bank Act is very important. I do not want to blame anybody, but I do not understand why it does not attract more interest, because it is the key. I would like to prove what I am saying. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most happy with the reaction of the Minister of Finance. I have had to make sacrifices in my life, when I needed these $10 and did not have them, when as a child I had to buy a three-cent stamp in order to be able to mail a letter to my mother and did not even have that much money, even though I was working 16 hours a day. Today, thanks to Providence, which has enabled me to come and sit in this House to speak out before my country in its highest forum, what I feel and what I wish for the future of our young generation, if the Minister of Finance wishes me to table my $10 bill with my document, I will agree to his requet and I would also like the bank note serial number to be recorded for posterity.
Mr. Speaker, why am I saying that? It is because we have reached a turning point in our history and that we find ourselves in a rather disturbing situation. Today, I was reading this article and I could perhaps table it but I will not ask for that because I would not want to try your patience, Mr. Speaker. I will just quote from the La Presse of March 22.
Portfolio managers do not know where to invest their money.
These people have problems with money because they just have too much of it. They do not know where to invest it. Yet on the other side the Minister of Finance is worried by a lack of capital needed to run our economy. He calls on the Japanese, the Swiss, the Germans. Yet, those Germans, who are people whom I like, were precisely those same people who were defeated twice, during World War I when I had members of my family fighting on the battlefields; these Germans who were again defeated during the last world war. They have finally been defeated and Canada participated with the allies in that war, which means that we won. But how come then, if we were among the victors, how come we have to kneel down before the vanquished in order to get loans, in order that they grant us the means to go on administering the country?
Mr. Speaker, those are questions we must very seriously consider. I am not accusing anyone in particular, neither this government nor the governments before, but we must absolutely think about this. Bill C-49 gives us an opportunity to fully consider, at the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, all the provisions of Bill C-15, Bill C-57 and another, the number of which I do not know, when it is put forward again.
Mr. Speaker, if this question was not important, Bill C-57 would have passed last year. Bill C-15 would now be ready for reporting by the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic matters. The members of that committee, however, are tremendous, and I commend them for that. They study the bill clause by clause, whether to consider allowing foreign banks to establish subsidiaries in Canada, which committee members are not ready to do-and I am in a position to know since I am a member of that committee-they are not ready to allow everything without a good look. All members of the committee-and the interim report that has been presented
Bank Act
will prove it-want to be absolutely sure, as members of the House and as members of the parliamentary committee, that not one recommendation in that report will have been made without due consideration.
Mr. Speaker, we must get off the beaten path. I propose to prepare a minority report. Perhaps hon. members will find that funny and will not take it too seriously. But we ought to be careful. Other people will be here when we are gone. Other people will read our decisions. They will analyse our debates and if we cannot take our responsibilities and propose basic amendments to Bill C-15 or to any other bill that will follow, we will be recognized as people who have been unable to assume responsibility.
Sometimes Canadians ask us "What do you propose to do?" So I tell them, as my leader, Mr. Caouette, has said so often in the House, that it is high time that the Canadian government gave our national bank-I see that my colleague over there is listening to me very carefully; actually, I am convinced that he shares our view-the Bank of Canada, the sole responsibility for cashing the nation's credit, that the chartered banks be called upon to ask the directors of the Bank of Canada for the necessary credits to serve the public sector, and that the Bank of Canada serve the needs of the public sector, with an accountability very similar to what it now has. I know that some frivolous people will say that will create inflation.
Mr. Speaker, what is the difference between putting $50 million in circulation through loans from the private bank system or through the Bank of Canada? What is the difference? The government and the departments could agree to reimburse the loans at a given annual interest rate and that rate would certainly be lower that what we are paying now. That has to be said time and time again, maybe some will say: You are always repeating the same thing. That is true! That is because we have a good memory. That is because we believe in the philosophy we advocate. The sun rises every morning. When it does not, when it is cloudy, people get concerned. It always does the same thing. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) smiling. I know that deep down he is saying to himself: That guy is not all that stupid. I am telling things as they are.
Mr. Speaker, I wish that for once we could stand up and analyse our banking system. I ask the Minister of Finance, who is present and whom I respect, that he consider seriously, with his advisers, introducing an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act so that this institution can play its true role as maker of the currency in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to note that Canadians can produce everything that is reported in statistics or earned in the gross national production of Canada, but we are too stupid to design a tool to measure values and exchanges so that we are compelled to borrow abroad. I asked some young people this week at a Canadian forum what was the difference between a $10 bill and a $2 bill. They replied intelligently that the figure 2

March 22, 1979
Bank Act
appears on the $2 bill and the figure 10 appears on the $10 bill. This is all the difference. They are only figures that appear on coins, bank notes and cheques. Our entire monetary system in Canada is made up of figures. There is certainly a serious shortage of figures in Canada if we have to borrow figures abroad and pay stupid interests on them.
Mr. Speaker, this is what I wanted to suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). I know he is a very busy man. The devaluation of the dollar which would be one of the consequences of the Social Credit system would lower the value of the Canadian dollar, according to us. I know he is concerned about inflation, another consequence of the system suggested by my party. If the Social Credit Party of Canada assumed power, we would experience inflation and the dollar would devaluate. If our system advocated the distribution of a better credit system in our country, there would be unemployment. We have unemployment, devaluation of the dollar and inflation, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to be spiteful because I know the Minister of Finance has enough problems. However, in all frankness, I would like to ask him at least to consider seriously our proposals and with his officials to try by all possible means to implement them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was speaking when the debate was adjourned at ten o'clock last Monday night. I wanted to come back to a particular point in that bill, more specifically clause 16. Now, if hon. members are willing to consider one aspect of the bill, I do not know what the subject will be of the order to be made on clause 15, but with regard to clause 16 we do know what I was opposed to, as well as my colleagues as I said the other night: that is, one of the provisions of Bill C-42, the act on the allocation of energy resources in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I shall be coming back to this over and over again, that is, to that particular point, and I shall take the government House leader to task on this point. We get closure more and more often.

I am glad to see that the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) has entered the House because my remarks in this instance will be addressed to him. I want to tell him that notwithstanding his jocular attitude this afternoon there is one aspect of his leadership of this House which is absolutely regrettable, which is a total minus quantity. As I said earlier this afternoon, it concerns procedures and changes of structure in this House required for the consideration not only of legislation but a variety of other matters.
For instance, there is the matter of the adjournment debate upon which there is agreement. There are a number of other
March 22, 1979

areas where there is total agreement. Either through lack of vigilance or through lack of militancy the government House leader has failed to respond. I hear the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) say "lack of time". No. There would be no debate on the matter; there would be agreement. But the committee has not met except to elect its executive, since 1977. I have been twice elected as vice-chairman. I have been chairman of that committee. The former member for Eglington has been chairman. The present minister for intergovernmental relations is the last chairman of that committee. I maintain that the committee should be meeting regularly to receive suggestions from hon. members, from the Chair and from the leadership with regard to the rules and practices of this House. To date it has been as worthwhile as that proverbial army which gets paraded up and down, up and down and cannot fight worth a damn. It has done absolutely nothing.
The hon. member may ask what this has to do with Bill C-38. Well, it has to do with this damned fool provision in the statute which deals with a negative resolution. I remember that when the hon. John Turner was minister of justice, before he became minister of finance, he brought down the act dealing with statutory instruments. We then saw for the first time the definition of affirmative and negative resolutions and the procedures for enabling them to be dealt with in this House or the other place. It was stated then that we would soon amend our procedures. That was over seven years ago.
So with Bill C-42, we get closure by statute. We are allowed five hours of debate when dealing with a negative resolution. Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough, and notwithstanding that we are being offered a 3 per cent reduction in federal sales tax, I would personally be prepared to vote against this bill on that ground alone because I think it makes a travesty of the proceedings of the House. I hold the government House leader totally responsible, because a long time ago a reference should have been made to the committee on this subject and the necessary procedural changes made so as to allow parliament to be master of its own rules. Here we are being told we must behave in the House according to a statute, and to my mind that is totally wrong.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN COUNCIL OF CHRISTIANS AND JEWS
speechtext:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all minutes of meetings, telegrams and letters having to do with any negotiations between the Department of the Secretary of State and the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews for the years 1976, 1977 and 1978.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on January 24 the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Daudlin) advised the House that the correspondence and documents which I had requested and which give details of negotiations, etc., about public grants between the government and the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews was, and I quote "too voluminous and would be inordinately time consuming and costly to prepare". I was absent on that date and I therefore extend my thanks to the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Papros-ki) for requesting that my motion be transferred for debate, because there is obviously a difference of opinion on the matter.
At the outset I wish to make it absolutely clear that I am in full agreement with the aims and principles of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews, an organization which had a very distinguished record under one of its former and very distinguished presidents, Dr. Richard Jones. I should emphasize that this is not the same man as, nor is he any relation to, Mr. Peter Jones, to whom I may refer in the course of my remarks and who has just resigned as president of the council.
It is a mystery to me why the government should seek to hide from public view a legitimate request for information concerning a matter which involves the expenditure of public money. In the last year alone this amounts to about three-quarters of a million dollars. How could such documents be so
4426

March 22, 1979
Canadian Council of Christians and Jews time consuming to produce? How could copies of such documents be so costly to prepare? I can only view this as a method of trying to cover up something which the government does not want made public. I can only view it as an attempt by the government to whitewash whatever it is that it does not want people to know. If this was not true, then the government would simply say to the House at the conclusion of my remarks today that it is quite prepared to produce all these documents on this matter in order to clear the air completely as a result of the numerous questions which have been asked.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) recently answered some questions I have had on the order paper since October 18 of last year, and in answer to question No. 294 he certainly severely misled the House-although I am absolutely certain it was not intentional on his part-when he stated, and I quote: "The accounts of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews are, of course, audited annually by the council's own auditors".
According to information I have, that is a complete misstatement of fact. To prove this, I draw attention to a copy of a letter which I have in my possession written by Yale and Partners, auditors for the city of Toronto. I think only one sentence of this letter needs to be read: "We have examined the combined balance sheet of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews". Therefore, the Secretary of State was wrong in saying that a full audit was conducted; there is certainly a tremendous difference between the examination of a balance sheet and a full audit. I think the minister well knows that fact.
I am surprised that the government should try to make political capital out of the fact that a member of the opposition questions the expenditure of public money, since that really is one of the many and very important reasons we are here in this House. The Secretary of State has sought to distort the entire issue through such means as issuing a press release containing incorrect information and, in effect, trying to paint me as someone who is besmirching public servants and who also apparently is opposed to Christians and Jews. I do not intend to tolerate and do not think any member should tolerate such uncalled for nonsense.
Here I would like to set the record straight on one point. An unfortunate error appeared in a Canadian Press story dated, I believe, February 28, 1979, which stated that I said outside this House that certain members of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews had paid kickbacks to members of the Department of the Secretary of State in order to receive grants. I did not at any time make such a statement with regard to members or the executive of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews. On being advised of this error in the Canadian Press story, I immediately asked that a correction be made.
I admit that I did demand on that date-and I still do-an examination, an investigation and an audit by the Auditor General of Canada with regard to this whole affair. I did state that in my view the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews should welcome such an audit in view of the allegations of kickbacks which were flying around Parliament Hill, so that

the air could be thoroughly cleared for all concerned. This is far different from the unfortunate report attributed to me that members of the council were supposedly committing illegal acts or engaging in illegal activities which, as far as I know, is absolutely not the case.
My request for a correction in the Canadian Press story stands as a matter of record. That request was made to the local representative of the Canadian Press in Brockville, Ontario, to the desk editor in the city of Toronto and to officials at its bureau here in Ottawa. As a result of the questions I raised and as a result of pressure from other sources as well, the government agreed to what the Secretary of State called an independent audit which, I understand, has been going on for a few days. I find it extremely strange that the minister has been unable to answer my order paper question or to make public by means of a statement the name of the auditing firm which is conducting the audit, which is supposed to be independent. I find it extremely strange also that the facilities of the Auditor General of Canada were apparently not used.
What does the Secretary of State think such an audit will show? Surely he does not think it will provide an answer to the questions I have raised in the House and which have been raised by many persons elsewhere as well. For example, I refer to outstanding order paper question No. 1,295 which I placed to obtain answers which will certainly not be shown in any audit and which are very pertinent to this case.
For the record, I would like briefly to paraphrase some of these questions. Did any directors receive bonus payments from the council at any time in the last three years, and did such payments come from government funds? What were the amounts of the cheques issued, who received them and what were they for? I have been told that they came directly from government grants and were supposedly for overtime work performed in connection with Open House Canada. Why did Air Canada issue a pass to Mr. Peter Jones, the ex-president of the council who resigned a week or two ago?
In case there is any doubt in this regard, I would like to quote from a letter, a copy of which I have on my desk, dated June 6, 1978, addressed to his colleagues, in which Mr. Peter Jones said: "Once again I would like to attend each regional annual meeting and have been assured that I can have an Air Canada free pass in order to do this.". Is it the policy of this government to give out free Air Canada passes to all charitable organizations, just to certain charitable organizations or just to this particular charitable organization?
Why did Peter Jones recently resign as president of the council? I would like to quote from a letter written by him, dated January 28, 1978, and addressed to all regional directors. I have a copy of this letter on my desk as well. It contains the following paragraph:
I am frankly unhappy that it could be said of us that the council and its staff are taking money from the federal government and doing nothing in return. No question that we have done everything that we could. Legally we are in the right. Morally 1 am not so sure.
March 22, 1979

What is the moral principle of which Mr. Peter Jones is not so sure? Why were such prominent Canadians as John Fisher, Joel Aldred, Alex Geddes and others thrown off the executive of the council, and why was the Ottawa regional office suddenly abolished overnight?
Referring to Mr. Geddes, a very respected businessman in the city of Toronto, I would like to quote from a letter dated January 26, 1979, to Messrs. Lockwood and Ronson, co-chairmen of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews. I have a copy of this letter on my desk as well. In doing so, I point out that Mr. Geddes was a member not only of the executive committee but a member of the finance committee of that organization. Here is one paragraph:
You may recall that 1 was concerned about financial control, not only of the day to day operations with reference to the cost of programs, TV commercials and other activities, but especially the proper control and full accounting of the various government grants that have been received by the council in the last two years. I still don't know the total of funds received from government grants, but would guess it is somewhere in the order of $750,000. I think proper reports should be made regarding the use of each grant.
Here is another paragraph:
I was also concerned about the capital reserve of $950,000 that the council had two or three years ago. What is the amount of this reserve today and what happens to the interest income from it?
Incidentally, speaking of that capital reserve, I have a copy of a financial statement issued by the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews which shows that this reserve of $950,000 had, for some unexplained reason, diminished as of November 8 of last year to $746,000. Obviously some of this money could have come from government grants and I cannot see why the Secretary of State should object to the asking of such obvious questions.
It could also be asked of the Secretary of State why he seems so totally unconcerned that the balance sheet of the council dated September 30, 1978, did not show the amount of money received from the Government of Canada-in other words, the taxpayers of Canada; nor does it show how it was dispensed, despite the fact that the sum involved, by the Secretary of State's own admission in answer to an order paper question of mine, ran to $767,000 in 1978 and $304,000 in 1977.
Mr. Peter Jones had admitted that he received a 4.5 per cent mortgage on his home from the council expiring May 13, 1981, and a loan reported to be interest-free in excess of $9,000 also received from the council. I have asked the legitimate question, which the Secretary of State has so far refused to answer, as to whether such funds came from government grants. Perhaps he cannot answer the question if all government grants go into the same bank account as other grants, because then any amounts removed for any purpose from those accounts such as those I have named would be partially public funds; and I believe that under the circumstances it should not be the intention of any government to donate money for a specific project that even in part ends up financing a home or a loan for a private individual.
Canadian Council of Christians and Jews
Why has the Secretary of State refused to confirm or deny that a meeting of regional directors of the council was held in Toronto last year at which the president, Mr. Peter Jones, instructed regional directors present on ways he thought they could avoid paying income tax to the Government of Canada on bonuses or on honorariums received? If this happened, it is reprehensible on the part of the government to ignore it. And why have such men as Gerry Yanover, legislative assistant to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), Paul Hellyer, journalist Max Keeping and numerous others severed their connections with this organization?
No, Mr. Speaker, the audit being conducted will not show the answer to these questions. It will be a whitewash covering up errors on the part of the government of a most serious nature, and perhaps to some extent a cover up which may have been, not dishonesty, but bad management on the part of Peter Jones, president of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews.
I would also like to mention that the CBC taped an interview with me and William White of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews which was scheduled for broadcasting on Monday, March 5, a week or two ago. This broadcast was never allowed on the air and I was offered the flimsiest excuses by the CBC as to why the broadcast did not go on as scheduled. Surely the Secretary of State, whose department is directly responsible for the CBC, had nothing to do with censorship of this kind, and I would ask him to give a full explanation to the House in this regard.
In the past few days a Mr. Dennis Flack has been in Ottawa on different occasions claiming to represent the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews. I might mention he is a former paid employee of the Liberal Party of Canada. I have been told by various sources, including members of parliament, that he has been attempting to call on both MPs and members of the cabinet. I understand, for example, that he did manage to see the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid) who, incidentally, raised this whole subject on the order paper before I did a year or more ago and before he was made a minister, and it is interesting to note that his own government would not even answer him. I do not object to Mr. Flack exercising the democratic right of lobbying, but it brings up the point as to who paid his expenses when he was here. I believe the Secretary of State should investigate this as well.
Referring back to the reported meeting in Toronto last year where Mr. Jones allegedly instructed regional directors on how to avoid paying income tax, I wonder if the Secretary of State is willing to determine from the Department of National Revenue whether the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews issued T-4 slips for such sums of money before the required deadline of February 28. I have been told that such slips were not issued, and while this may or may not be correct, I certainly think it should be clarified.
In conclusion, I feel there is no justification for the government not to agree now, in the absence of the Secretary of State, to having whoever is representing him here in the House rise and state that the government has had a change of heart

March 22, 1979
Canadian Council of Christians and Jews
and that all documents, correspondence and anything pertaining to the negotiations between the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews and the Government of Canada in regard to government grants be made public; in other words, that the original request which I made on the order paper be granted. Surely the Secretary of State, who is usually a reasonable man, or his representative will now rise and offer to clear the air by allowing the necessary documents to be made public without further delay and in the interests of all concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest this afternoon to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) in the hope that he might do something more than the left-handed attempt to extricate himself from the innuendo and subterfuge which he used to taint both the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews and the Department of the Secretary of State in this matter.
It would only be appropriate if I pointed out to members of the House the method whereby this matter has come forward. The hon. member opposite has become expert in raising this matter on a number of occasions by motions under Standing Order 43, implying thereby that something terrible was happening and making unsubstantiated and unsupported allegations that something terrible was happening, but not following them up with any question, notwithstanding the fact that following these motions under Standing Order 43 there were periods of weeks in which the hon. member had the occasion to follow up on these allegations and put questions. But no questions were put, leaving the innuendoes and the allegations to be picked up by the public at large with no opportunity being given to answer them.
I sat here on a number of occasions in the absence of my minister hoping and waiting for the hon. member to rise in his place and put his money where his mouth is by asking questions which I would have been prepared to answer. But the questions never came. What was left was innuendo and the suggestion that something must be wrong. Again today the hon. member stood in his place and suggested that all kinds of things must be happening because he has not had a response to his questions.
On January 24 I rose in my place and indicated that there would have to be substantial costs, time and effort beyond what should be reasonable to answer a question of this type. The hon. member indicated that he was not satisfied and implied that there was something to be whitewashed and covered up. Now the hon. member says that the article was wrong. I assume this is the first time he has said this. I have seen no other occasions. I have seen nothing in Hansard. I assume this is the first time the hon. member has stood up and indicated publicly in the House that in fact the newspaper article was wrong. He has left from the time of the newspaper article until now the impression that it was not wrong.
