Mr. Speaker, the hon. member makes a point.
I could research for him and provide documentation where on a number of occasions members from both sides of the House have used an opportunity in the House to rise and indicate that they have been misquoted outside the House. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting that that has not been done or the opportunity does not exist. Had the hon. member used the opportunity of a question or a motion under Standing Order 43 to suggest the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews in fact was being blamed for something they ought not be blamed for as a result of a misquote, I am sure all members of the House would have been happy to see him rise. But that did not happen.
I find it passing strange, after having disclaimed that he had made any allegations of kickback, that the hon. member would say immediately that the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews should have been anxious to respond to all the allegations going around on the hill that there had been kickbacks. By whom were they made if not by the hon. member? Yet the hon. member said that he did not say it. In the same article he is quoted as supposedly trying to disclaim that he had said anything but "Of course, I don't have any information". The hon. member has not disclaimed that it was true.
I suggest this procedure has been used very effectively by the member: to have no information, to have no background knowledge, but to make unsubstantiated allegations and then suggest through the smokescreen that something terrible must be happening.
In anticipation of the audit showing that everything was on the up and up and correctly done, the hon. member has sown seeds to suggest the audit will bring forward nothing. Even if it comes forward and proves there was no malfeasance and nothing to support the innuendo left by the hon. member, he is sowing seeds to suggest it will prove nothing, that it was a whitewash.
I respectfully suggest that almost from a sense of paranoia the hon. member thinks that not only is the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) against him, but also his agencies because they did not choose to use an interview between himself and some other person. It is ludicrous.
I and other members of the House find it particularly distressing that any hon. member should-and I use the word carefully-carelessly and with a self-confessed total lack of truth in effect vilify members of the public service. The hon. member is disclaiming now that he intended that, but it was the effect. He talked about cause and effect. That was the effect of what he left in the open press. Also it is distressing that he should vilify members of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews by making the allegations which he now disclaims.
March 22, 1979

On March 6 the Secretary of State told members that he had received a request by telegram from the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews, both protesting against the irresponsibility of these statements and asking that an independent audit be made of their activities so that it could be shown the allegations are baseless. It is on record that the council is doing what it can to dissociate itself from the type of allegations which have been made. In light of those requests and the immediate affirmative reaction by the Secretary of State, it should be obvious to all hon. members that the council is not only acting in good faith, but is satisfied its activities place it above this particularly odious type of suspicion. Of course, the audit will find that members of the Department of the Secretary of State at all times have carried on negotiations with the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews in an irreproachable manner. It will establish once and for all that the activities of the council are faultless regarding the use of government funds.
Despite the time and costs involved, research is being undertaken with all dispatch to provide ultimate proof that all parties are beyond reproach in this unfortunate incident. I should like to advise the hon. member that when the results are produced, and as they are being produced by the department for the independent audit, they will be made available to him.
They will be placed before the House, at which time I am satisfied all members will see they had just reason for having confidence not only in the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews but in the Secretary of State.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to hear an hon. member suggest that this bill should pass without further debate. He probably realizes, as do other members of the House, that more has been sneaked through in this bill than with most pieces of legislation. It is a complicated bill. The fact that we will deal with it in committee of the whole gives members an opportunity to deal with specific clauses. It is an omnibus type of bill that does a lot of things to a lot of people.
I want to deal with one clause tonight which concerns the implementation of an increased air transportation tax and ultimate conversion to user charges. We have here a classic example of the application of the user-pay concept without "user say". We have a situation where the airlines are being asked to pay for the services provided by the Department of Transport, some of which are required, some of which are extravagant, and some of which are not needed.
I do not think anyone would argue that airlines and passengers who use them should not pay for the realistic services and facilities provided. The government is asking for more than that, however. In effect it is asking the Canadian travelling public to pay for the mistakes of overbuilding and extravagance of many airport facilities in this country. The Air Transportation Association of Canada has argued for some time that they have not had any meaningful input with regard to the facilities they require. The Department of Transport builds without meaningful consultation and, as a result, there is a constant conflict of opinion about the services that are provided and the services that are needed, and who is to pay for them.
The Air Transport Association of Canada represents the vast majority of airlines in this country-85 per cent or 90 per

March 22, 1979
Excise Tax Act
cent of them. It states that they are the victims in this process and, by virtue of the fact that they are the victims, they have no choice but to hand the cost on to the public. They contend that they are the captive tenants of a monopolistic landlord. In a bulletin dated February 22, referring to the air transportation tax and its conversion to a user charge, the association had this to say:
Airline passengers in Canada will shortly be paying a tax which will be typically $15 per flight-
That is an increase from the $8 we presently pay-almost 100 per cent.
The bulletin continues:
-following the government's budget announcement that it would increase the present tax by nearly 100 per cent. This unwarranted and abusive treatment of the airline traveller has taken place at the same time as the Task Force on Tourism has strongly recommended government measures to reduce the cost of travel.
In addition to the monstrous increase in the tax, the government has stated its intention to convert the tax to a user charge to be levied upon the air carriers under the Aeronautics Act. The estimated yield of the new tax rate is approximately $150 million annually.
The major air carriers affected have carefully considered the matter and state they are unable to absorb such an amount into their cost base or their market expectations, and are therefore firmly opposed to the planned conversion of the tax.
The carriers will not willingly be parties to a conversion device which would hide from parliament and the public the consequences of the government's reluctance to pare the costs of the DOT bureaucracy and instead contribute significantly to further increases in air travel costs.
In essence, that lays the groundwork for the points I wish to cover tonight. This government has been on a building binge and now it wants to implement a scheme of cost recovery. It will collect from the carrier, but in turn the carrier will collect from the passenger. I contend that users should not have to pay for the grandiose schemes, the Taj Mahals, the overbuilding, and art work, and all the unnecessary frills included in today's modern terminal buildings.
We hear a lot about restraint, Mr. Speaker, but we have to ask ourselves whether restraint has been a part of the over-all managerial plan of the Department of Transport. When we look at the estimates we have to answer in the negative. No fat has been trimmed in the estimates of the Department of Transport, particularly in connection with air transport administration. The deputy minister of transport took a great deal of pride in saying that the detrimental effects on the continuing operations of the department were minimal, that there was very little disruption to the job security of Transport Canada employees.
We all remember that in the restraint program it was proposed that $200 million be shaved off the operations of DOT, some $130 million of which shows in cutbacks in program expenditure and $70 million of which is incorporated in this legislation. This is the first time a suggested saving has led to the imposition of a further tax.
The department has reduced the person-years requirements by a mere 87 persons for air administration. Some 13,000 person-years are involved in the operations of the air administration of the Department of Transport so we have not seen
[Mr. Mazankowski.J
any real evidence of cutbacks in the operations of the air administration branch of the Department of Transport. Again I ask why the travelling public should have to pay for the failure of the administration to make reasonable cutbacks. We know there has been a growing bureaucracy. We know many of the programs could have been shaved, but why should the travelling public be asked to pay for the mismanagement of the department?
I should like to quote some passages from the 100th Annual Report of the Auditor General of Canada to the House of Commons for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1978. It contains an in-depth audit of the Department of Transport, and at page 503 there is the following statement:
Our audits disclosed serious deficiencies in the systems and procedures the department used in acquiring capital assets in the projects we examined. Five of the projects did not achieve a reasonable standard of 'due regard for economy.'
This is the conclusion of a person this House holds in high regard, whose integrity cannot be questioned, and who has done a very objective and in-depth analysis of the situation. Perhaps it is no wonder that in a rather unique statement, certainly not something one would be very proud of, the deputy minister of transport suggested the Auditor General stick to auditing rather than criticizing the department. He said that he warned the Auditor General. J. J. Macdonell, against claiming too much management .erritory. Deputy Minister Sylvain Cloutier said the Auditor General runs the risk of turning himself into a management consultant or adviser, rather than sticking to the job he is supposed to do- auditing.
One of the duties given to the Auditor General by this House was a mandate to examine whether public funds were being spent on behalf of the Canadian people having due regard to economy and efficiency. The Auditor General is clearly within his mandate in making those kinds of judgments and assessments. Someone has to protect the public purse. Parliament has lost control; the Auditor General pointed that out. The government has lost control. Surely we need someone who can examine in an objective way whether the principles of accounting and good management are adhered to. It is unfortunate that a senior public servant would lash out at a man who is attempting to protect the public purse and ensure that some of the deficiencies within the management and control systems of the Government of Canada are upgraded, improved, and made more effective.
The Auditor General identified several other serious deficiencies within the Ministry of Transport. I refer here to the capital cost overruns which he cited. Here again are clear examples of the failure of the Ministry of Transport to provide a reasonable standard of due regard for economy and efficiency. The construction of the Calgary airport is one example. Its costs escalated from $57 million to $127 million, which is two and a half times the original amount. The comments which the Auditor General made confirm my remarks that there has not been meaningful consultation with the people who will be using such terminals. At page 506 of his report, in reference to
March 22, 1979

the Calgary International Airport the Auditor General stated as follows:
The air carriers expressed strong reservations as to the immediate need for, and concern about the cost of, new terminal facilities.
This is a very important statement. The airlines were concerned about the cost of the new terminals and that they did not need that sort of facility at that time because they knew that eventually someone would have to pay for it.
At page 507 the Auditor General says:
In our opinion, the Department of Transport did not give due regard to economy in the Calgary airport project.
The concerns expressed by the air carriers were not disclosed. The Auditor General goes on to say at page 507:
The Department did not reach agreement with the air carriers on user-pay cost-recovery charges until just prior to the opening of the new terminal.
Further on in the same paragraph he says:
In our view, reaching an agreement on cost-recovery charges prior to the start of construction was essential to ensure concern for economy and discourage any unjustified user demands.
The users, in this case the airlines, did not have an opportunity for meaningful input in the construction of that facility. The Auditor General examined the costs of the Calgary airport. I wonder what would have happened if he had examined the costs of the Mirabel airport which have escalated dramatically. It is costing now in the order of $1 million per week in terms of its operational deficit. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a clear example of mismanagement and irresponsibility on the part of government and of the people in charge at the Ministry of Transport. That is why we are being asked to approve a bill which will give MOT the authority literally to double the airport tax.
At the same time we are creating a huge airport revolving fund so that some of these white elephants can be hidden and so allow the spending spree to carry on. In that connection the Air Transport Association of Canada has this to say:
This cross subsidizing group of 23 airports would be able to generate about $100 million yearly from its own cash flow. This would pay for most capital expansion, and make the group effectively independent of parliamentary appropriations.
They go on to talk about ministerial powers as follows:
The Canadian commercial airline industry is alarmed and deeply concerned that the minister's power to make charges under the Aeronautics Act is not counterbalanced by any regulatory body.
It is not counterbalanced by any regulatory body because if there were a meaningful regulatory body wherein there could be the opportunity for the airlines, in this case the users, to have some meaningful input and negotiations to work out the type of user fees, and to have some input in determining what is the best kind of facility to build, and where it should be built, we would not have nearly the problem we have in terms of meeting the cost overruns and in terms of meeting operational deficits.
The Air Transport Association of Canada says it believes that legislative amendments should be considered that would subject the minister's powers to make charges to the same tests of fairness and reasonableness applied to air carriers' fare
Excise Tax Act
proposals. In other words, they are saying that they have to go before the CTC any time they want an increase in fares. There is a check or balance there. There is no check or balance here on the minister in charge, or on the bureaucracy who initiate the kind of user fees that they deem necessary with which to pay the bill.
We should look briefly at the impact of these increased charges. In addition to the impact of the airport user charge, which we have known it as, there are also some very significant increases being implemented at the same time over an eight-year period respecting landing fees, general terminal fees, the en route North Atlantic fees, and almost every service that is provided.
I have a breakdown of the cost of landing a Boeing 747 in Toronto. These figures are based on October 1, 1978, data. I put these figures on the record so hon. members can be apprised of what it costs to land a jumbo jet. The particular example I will give is of a transoceanic flight with a full passenger load. The costs include the en route North Atlantic fee in the amount of $130; the landing fee amounting to $1,596; the general terminal fee assessed at $267; security charge for 429 passengers at 20 cents per passenger amounting to $86; and the fuel throughput charge for 22,000 gallons at 1.5 cents per gallon, amounting to $330. Then we have a provincial fuel tax on 22,000 gallons at three cents per gallon, which amounts to $660, and a transportation tax, 429 passengers at $8, which amounts to $3,432. When you total all those together, and it does not take into consideration the rental of the airline space for counters and so on, it works out to $6,501 to land a 747 with 429 passengers aboard. Those are the rates effective October 1, 1978.
The impact of the transportation tax at $15 per person will change that $3,432 figure to $6,435. The immediate 30 per cent increase which is going to be imposed on an annual basis over an eight-year period when these new landing fees are going to be implemented, will increase that $6,500 figure to $9,604. Those are the kinds of increases about which we are talking.
The principal element in the plan is essentially to allow domestic landing fees and related fees to rise at a rate of 30 per cent on an annual basis to about six times their present level over an eight-year period. That is the goal of the department. We are looking at something that is very significant.
I can point out as well that the general terminal fee will be increased at the rate of 25 per cent effective April 1, 1979, 50 per cent effective October 1, 1979, and 100 per cent effective April 1, 1980. Therefore we will have a doubling of the terminal fees which will parallel this particular measure. At a time when we are talking about cheaper air fares in this country with the airlines being asked to trim the frills, cut the fat, and provide a more efficient operation, we have some of the basic ingredients of the cost of air travel provided by the government being increased dramatically.

March 22, 1979
Excise Tax Act
I talked about the commercial passenger and the impact that this measure will have upon the traveller who lands in Toronto, Montreal, Edmonton or Calgary. There is another impact which I am sure the government and the minister have overlooked. Air travel in some areas of the country is the only mode of travel. I talk here particularly about the north.
I have a letter from the Yellowknife Chamber of Commerce. In addition to having an exchange of correspondence with me, I am sure they directed the same correspondence to the minister. I quote from their letter of December 13:
As you are aware, the majority of Northwest Territories communities are served solely by air, and because of this the federal tax on air transportation is unfair to Northwest Territories residents. We often have no choice but to fly, and are therefore stuck with a tax that we have no choice but to pay. At least in southern centres this tax is "voluntary"-one need not pay the tax if an alternate to air transport is used.
At present, the air transportation tax from Northwest Territories airports is gaining approximately $480,000 per year for the federal treasury, and a total of $900,000 per year can be expected after the proposed increase. This must surely represent the highest per capita revenue from any province or territory for this tax-largely because we have no choice but to fly.
Because this tax increases the cost of an essential service in the Northwest Territories, and is therefore unfair, the Yellowknife Chamber of Commerce strongly urges the repeal of the air transportation tax in the Northwest Territories.
I thank you for your consideration of this matter and hope that we can look forward to your interceding on our behalf to have this tax removed.
Yours truly,
Fred Richinger
I have, as well, a letter from the Northwest Territories Association of Municipalities which says essentially the same thing. I quote:
Eighty-two per cent of our population and ninety per cent of our municipalities have no choice but to use aircraft for year round access to communities other than their own.
The north has received little benefit (proportionate to our geographic size) to compare with the federal subsidies enjoyed by Canada's transportation network; i.e. seaways, highways, canals, railways, airlines, shipbuilding and airport facilities.
This form of tax is regressive in that it applies to all users regardless of their means. In Canada's north air travel is not a luxury but the only means of transportation available to the majority of us.
That is essentially the thrust and the feeling of those who will be faced with this abusive tax. It will be more harsh for them because they have no alternate form of transportation. Travel by air is certainly not a luxury as far as they are concerned.
I said at the outset that we are concerned about our tourist trade deficit. The Air Transport Association of Canada made reference to that in their submissions which they have made public. I wish to place on record some quotations from the government's own report by the sector task force on the Canadian tourist industry. We all know there is a huge deficit in our tourist trade. Many attempts are being made to try to turn that deficit around.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and other federal government departments are devising ways and means and coming up with all sorts of schemes to
[Mr. Mazankowski.)
attract more tourist trade to Canada and to prevent our tourist dollars flowing outside the country. On the other hand we have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Department of Transport imposing their user-pay program which is generally going to militate against that desire. It really is an uncoordinated approach.
It is not the first time this government has adopted that kind of stance. It has happened many times. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is devoted to overcoming regional economic disparity. At the same time the Ministry of Transport is imposing user-pay because it does not feel transportation is an instrument for overcoming regional economic disparities. The two departments are working against one another. It is time the government got its act together.
I will quote from this report because it is very significant. If the government followed the advice that its own study has revealed, it may be able to get its act together and work toward reversing or at least abating the current tourist trade deficit. I quote from page 28 of the report:
Apropos the Canadian Transport Commission, the task force recommends that existing CTC policies should be reviewed to ensure that, whilst these regulations govern all air travel within, to and from Canada, prominent importance is given to air transport as a vehicle to increase and improve tourism travel to and within Canada.
No one would argue with that, I am sure.
Discussions should be held with all interested parties concerned with those regulations of a potentially restrictive nature.
Then we get into the user-pay policy and the airport user tax. I quote again:
The airport user-pay policy makes air transportation in Canada non-competitive with that of the United States and is detrimental to Canadian tourism development.
Nothing can be clearer than that, and this report was published before the minister brought down his budget.
I quote again:
The industry is in general agreement with the principle of the necessary functional requirements being paid for by users whenever economically justifiable. However, governments should assume all costs related to social and/or regional development of facilities. Airports can be classified as full-recovery, partial-recovery or nil-recovery.
These are important recommendations. Living as we do in a country which is widespread and sparsely populated, we should consider them very carefully. If that recommendation were adopted we could expect a greater measure of fairness and equity, particularly for people who reside in isolated areas such as the north.
I quote again:
Anything in excess of necessary functional requirements should not be paid for by the users, for example, art work. The users must have a very strong voice in what are defined as functional requirements. All users, including carriers, concessionaires and the travelling public, as well as the general public, should share the burden of paying for functional requirements. The existing CTC policy should be reviewed to ensure that while the regulations govern all air travel within, to and from Canada, prominent importance is given to air transport as a vehicle to increase and improve tourism travel to and within Canada. Discussions
March 22, 1979

should be held with all interested parties concerned with those regulations which are of a potentially restrictive nature.
Sir, that is a good summary of the situation we are now facing. I repeat, users of airport services should be prepared to pay their fair share. They should be prepared to pay for the services needed to provide efficient and safe air transportation. But they should not be asked to pay for the government's bungling, mismanagement, waste and incompetence. Nor should the travelling public be asked to pay for the expensive tastes of the ministry and the bureaucrats.
I submit that this tax imposes a penalty which will hurt the tourist industry and the Canadian traveller. This detrimental approach of attempting total cost recovery should be thoroughly re-examined and this measure should be withdrawn.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House tonight covers a number of important items. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has talked about one of them, namely, the airport tax. I should like the minister to give us a fuller explanation with regard to the manufacturing sales tax cut.
As we all know, the tax was cut from 12 per cent to 9 per cent in the budget last November. A lot of optimism was expressed at the time that the decrease would be passed on to the consumer. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) has told us many times that his department is monitoring this situation, that CSIP was monitoring it, that the AIB was monitoring it, and that all would be well. As recently as a few days ago, however, the minister told us that his study was not yet complete, that the monitoring process was still continuing. I should like him to tell us tonight what kind of investigation is being carried out and whether it is, in fact, nearing completion. Who is being surveyed? Will the minister undertake to table the report in the House when he receives it, if there is time before an election, so that the Canadian people may see it?
I ask this because when it was introduced last fall the sales tax cut was worth about $1 billion to manufacturing companies and a great deal of concern has been expressed by consumer associations and related groups that it is not being passed on. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on November 24 just after the budget was introduced. Some Montreal retailers were quoted as saying they doubted very much whether the cut would be passed on-they believed it would be absorbed in the pricing structure between the wholesaler and the consumer.
Montreal retailers say it is doubtful consumers will see lower prices in the wake of last week's cut to 9 per cent from 12 per cent in the federal sales tax.
The cut, a part of Finance Minister Jean Chretien's budget, affects the tax that manufacturers pay to the government as they sell their goods at the factory gate-usually to a wholesaler.
By the time the retailer gets the goods, the federal sales tax is included in the price. So retailers say they would lose money if they cut prices on inventory purchased before Chretien's budget announcement.
They add they would only cut prices if their competitors did so and forced them to match prices.
Excise Tax Act
So retailers in Montreal were suggesting that consumers might not reap the benefit which was intended for them by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
There are other statistics which lead one to suspect that the sales tax cut is not being passed on. A couple of days ago the Globe and Mail said corporate profits had gone up by 46 per cent in the last week of 1978. We are not against people making a fair profit, Mr. Speaker, but we cannot help wondering whether the reason, or part of the reason, for this tremendous increase in profits might not have been companies retaining the advantage of the tax cut. Then again, a few days ago the industrial price index for manufacturing was released. The increase was 11 per cent or a little more, the highest recorded in a number of years. That figure is for February and it is very high, especially when one considers that inventories must have been largely depleted by February, that the sales tax must by then have been removed from those inventories to the extent of 3 per cent, and that the reduction should have been reflected in the selling price.
In my opinion the Minister of Finance has been a lot stronger than the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in trying to defend the validity of the cut. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said about a week ago that the CPI showed that in January the price of clothing had dropped, or, if it had not dropped, that it had levelled off. This, he indicated, was evidence that the cut was fulfilling its purpose. I pointed out to the minister that the manufacturing sales tax does not apply to clothing, food, drugs or heating fuel, so he had to think of another argument. When the minister speaks tonight I would like him to give us a few more details about what evidence he has that this sales tax cut is being passed on to the consumer. That is really all I am asking.
In his budget speech last November the minister said:
I estimate that the cut in the sales tax will reduce the increase in the consumer price index by one half of one per cent.
Back in November the consumer price index was at an annual rate of 8.7 per cent. The latest increase in the consumer price index, which was February over February, was some 9.2 per cent. There has been an increase of one half of one per cent in the consumer price index since the minister reduced the sales tax. On the surface it appears that the sales tax has not been passed on. I admit to the minister that all the arguments I am giving him are superficial, general, and global, because we in the opposition do not have at our disposal all the facilities, money and staff required to investigate properly whether the sales tax cut has been passed on to the consumer as it should have been. That is why I want to know what kind of study is under way, who is being surveyed, what the evidence is, and what proof the government has that the sales tax cut is being passed on to the consumer as it should be. That is the first and principal point I wanted to make in the debate tonight.
As has been said by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and by the hon. member for Vegreville, this

March 22, 1979
Excise Tax Act
bill includes a number of items besides the sales tax cut, which is by far the major item in the bill. There is an increase in the airport tax. People flying within Canada and outside will find that the transportation tax will go up to 15 per cent as of April 1. Like the hon. member for Vegreville, I do not think that type of tax is proper. It is a user-pay tax. People using airport facilities have to pay a tax when they take flights regardless of their ability to pay.
The ways and means bill before the House today includes a number of other measures. It includes the elimination of a special tax on private aeroplanes, the elimination of a tax on motorcycles, and the elimination of a tax on boat motors. It deals with non-commercial aviation fuel.
The bill also includes excise tax schedules for diesel fuel and gasoline, measurements of which are now being converted from the old imperial system to metric. It includes other things which I think are perhaps inconsequential. With the exception of the air transportation tax I think they are really not too important to the average Canadian, but things like the change to the metric system should be scrutinized closely in order to make sure that companies do not take advantage of the switch from the gallon to the litre in order to up their prices by a penny or a fraction of a penny.
I think some items in this bill would cause hardship for a number of people. One specific item has to do with storm doors and windows, which previously were exempted from tax when the government reduced the tax on building materials some time ago from 12 per cent to 5 per cent. The tax on storm doors and windows was removed, and the bill before us re-imposes a 5 per cent tax on storm doors and windows.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I have here a telegram sent to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), which says:
The Quebec Provincial Wood Industry Association, representing the interest of the 450 door and window manufacturers of Quebec, strongly protests against the imposition of the 5 per cent tax on materials exempted since 1975.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that the government's decision is unfair. There has been no consultation with the firms involved and no reason has been advanced to justify that change. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the government will go back on its decision and abolish the tax on windows and doors. [English]
A number of industries, some of them being small companies, could be affected in a very negative way by this bill.
There is only one other point 1 want to make in my brief remarks. I think it is very important. Within the bill is a form of closure. I believe that was referred to by one hon. member who spoke previously in the debate. Clause 16(4) at page 12 of Bill C-38 states:
A motion taken up and considered in accordance with subsection (3) shall be debated without interruption for not more than five hours and, on the conclusion of such debate or at the expiry of the fifth such hour, the Speaker of the House of Commons or the Senate, as the case may be, shall forthwith, without further debate or amendment, put every question necessary for the disposal of the motion.
As I understand it, this refers to various orders in council which are referred to in clause 15 and in the schedules on pages 11 and 12 of the bill. I hope the minister will be prepared to answer questions in the committee of the whole and to tell us why this form of closure is included in the bill.

Again. It is very similar to the closure in the energy bill we debated a few days ago. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) moved a motion to remove that terrible provision from that bill, and we supported that. This bill also imposes automatic closure. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), and I concur in the statements made by both those hon. members. I hope not to get into the points they raised because they were very well made by both hon. members. I will attempt to confine my remarks to the parts of the bill which deal with energy, cars and trucks.
This bill is a result of the budget of November, some four and a half months ago, and this is the first time we have debated it. We see that the most important part of the bill, the reduction of the sales tax, is something that the government cannot explain. The government is unable to tell us whether the benefits are getting down to the people whom the sales tax cuts are supposed to benefit, that is, the consumers. Members of the House have asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) whether these sales tax cuts will get down to the consumers, and he told us we should have confidence in the marketplace. It is the government that has set down these policies and it is the government that should be accountable for them and responsible for how these policies operate.
I agree with the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) must respond in the House on his policies. When he states that the consumer price index

March 22, 1979

should be down by half a point because of the cut in the sales tax, he should tell us whether or not that is the case and whether he is making the studies to show that corporations, which are in the business of competing and are also in the business of making profits, are passing these cuts down to the people who should benefit from them.
I have had an ongoing discussion with the Minister of Finance regarding solar equipment and whether he would be in favour of granting a tax credit for putting it in place so that people could take advantage of it. I see in the bill that the excise tax on solar water heaters has been removed. This is a starting point, although a very small one, and we are concerned about the conservation of energy in this nation. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has been telling us all last week that a crisis would be imminent if another country were to cut off oil supplies to Canada, and that the government should be concerned about alternate forms of energy and how they can be put in place. One of those alternate forms is solar water heaters. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) stated that solar heat is one of the most promising areas of energy conservation in this country, and I agree with him.
In the government document entitled "Energy Futures for Canadians" the following statement is made:
The penetration of renewable resources to the extent shown would be a noteworthy accomplishment since most of the renewables lack any significant organizational, financial or market base at the present time. To establish so large a market for the renewables, individually and collectively, in so short a time presents Canadians with a major challenge, but one which has a high priority. By the year 2000, renewables would be contributing as much as imported oil at that time, or more than four times the energy currently supplied by nuclear power in Canada-a prodigious undertaking in 20 years.
These are very fine statements, but that is all they are, statements, because with the present policies in place there is absolutely no way we can achieve that use of renewables which is stated in government policy to be likely to take place by the year 2000. What we need is a policy which will encourage people to use solar equipment.
For example, a collector for a solar water heater costs $800 or $900, depending on whether you place the collector on your roof or on a pedestal. Then you must add pumps or controls, and this will add another $600 to the cost, making it around $1,500. Then you have to instal these facilities. Perhaps a number of people would be able to instal them themselves, but most would not, and when it is done totally by the commercial people it adds another $500 to the cost of the installation. So we are looking at an investment of some $2,000.
The government has removed the excise tax on equipment which, I suppose, would come from the United States and be developed here in Canada. That excise tax may save the consumer some $30, $40 or $50 at the most, but that is not a sufficient incentive for him to instal a solar water heater in his home. What we need is a tax credit which I have announced in the House to be the policy of the Progressive Conservative party. I fully believe that if the government were prepared to offer such a tax credit we would have a sufficient usage of renewables to reach the goals announced in the government's
Excise Tax Act
study, and thus would save a good deal of oil and gas which are becoming more and more expensive.
Also, as regards solar water heaters, we find that not all the equipment is made here in Canada. For example, the heat exchanger must be brought in from the United States. The reason for that is that the Canadian market is not sufficiently significant for Canadian manufacturers to go into the business of manufacturing these heat exchangers. The only way in which that could come about would be if greater consumption of those products were encouraged in Canada. As I said, in my opinion there is only one way to do that. Also, we must have a co-ordinated policy to develop more high technology necessary to develop the renewables, particularly the solar panels and collectors, so that we set down policies which encourage Canadian manufacturers to take advantage of them.
I was interested in the figures which showed that our higher technology and manufactured imports in 1978 amounted to some $29.3 billion. We have exported higher technology equipment worth $20 billion. That means we had a deficit in 1978 in the higher technology products of some $9.1 billion. I think that speaks for itself. It means that the government has a long way to go to encourage more research in this country to develop the kind of technology which must be made available to the consumers of those products. It is necessary if we are to promote such things as solar water heaters in our homes.
As I understand it, the excise tax is a tax on luxuries. I do not want to get back to the subject of renewables, but the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) pointed out that what the government is doing through the bill is to designate transportation as a luxury because it is putting a tax on it. As has been stated by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), we have a deficit of some $1.7 billion in the tourist trade in this nation. Surely he must have something to say about the user-pay concept that is in the bill and the increase in the landing tax. I would be interested to hear the Minister of Finance explain the reasoning behind that provision in view of the fact that we are concerned about decreasing our tourist deficit.
I referred previously to research and development which are so necessary to increase some of the high technology items needed in this country. Some months ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced this great program called PUSH which was to assist in the purchase and use of solar energy items, and I assumed that this would include solar water heaters in government buildings. He announced that in the years 1979 to 1984 he would make available some $125 million for the government to purchase solar energy and renewable energy items for government buildings. We find that even though the minister is still bragging about this program the department has now decided that the first $25 million, which should have been made available this year, will be only $1.5 million. We will be watching very closely whether the department is serious about this program or whether it is just another big announcement, using big figures, so that the people of this country will be made to believe that something is

March 22, 1979
Excise Tax Act
being done to help in these higher technology areas. But, in fact, nothing is happening.
When we talk about the use of energy and the conservation of it, we find that the minister removed the tax on solar water heaters and in the next clause he added on the tax to storm windows and doors. Surely this makes no sense. I cannot understand why the minister would do that. It cannot amount to very much money. I know people in the country are concerned about the conservation of energy in their homes and that they will be buying those materials anyway. It is beyond me why the department and the minister would attempt to save energy by removing a tax in one clause and adding it on again in the next. I want to question the minister on that in committee.
The last area I should like to speak about is the removal of the federal sales tax on trucks and cars. This tax was placed in a budget some years ago, and now the minister has decided that it was insignificant to the saving of energy and that it should be removed. We are all purchasers of new cars and trucks, and we welcome that move. But by announcing it one night, the minister has placed a number of dealers in situations where their inventories on hand are open to $200 to $300 per car, and more per truck. Dealers have had to advance sales on their inventories, and now they find the price of those cars and trucks must come down because consumers are demanding it. Thus they are caught with these inventories. If a dealer had 30 or 40 cars on his lot, which many of them did at the time of the budget, this could amount to anywhere from $5,000 to $10,000 which he must absorb himself. I am referring to an average small dealer.
Many dealers wrote to me and indicated that the tax cut should have been made retroactive so that they would not have to absorb it. They are the whim of the Minister of Finance as he adds on taxes and takes taxes off. No one seems to worry about the small businessman who must absorb these losses, or perhaps losses of sales because he is incapable of absorbing them. I have received a number of letters from dealers in my constituency. I know members on both sides of the House of Commons have received those letters. It is another question the Minister of Finance should answer when asked in committee. He should be asked whether he is prepared to deal with this loss for small businessmen.
There are a number of items in this bill which affect small businesses and individuals. We will be very interested in the answers the minister brings forward in committee.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that it is over four months since the budget of November 16. One must spend quite a bit of time refreshing one's memory on what was said at the time. It is interesting it took the minister over four months to get his bills before the House. I know the minister is a senior one in some people's books. We look to him to correct the errors we find in certain areas of legislation when ministers such as the Minister of

National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) are powerless to give people the relief they need in certain cases.
Essentially Bill C-38 covers three major areas: the air transportation tax, the gasoline tax, and the sales tax. I noted especially that the minister said in his budget speech he would repeal the special 10 per cent excise tax on marine engines over 20 horsepower and private aircraft, and the 5 per cent tax on motorcycles. He said that they were having an adverse economic effect. Also he indicated that the contribution of these taxes to energy conservation has been minimal. I guess the minister finally found out what taxpayers were telling members of parliament, at least on this side of the House. Regardless of the taxing policies of the Liberal government, people require boats which have more than 20 horsepower engines. One cannot move a ship which weighs hundreds of tons with a tiny motor. One requires an acceptable size motor. I suppose efficiency is related to the relative size of the motor and the vessel being moved. It should not have come as any surprise to the minister that the contribution of these taxes to energy conservation had been minimal.
As far as the tax on private aircraft is concerned, perhaps the minister realized finally that there was quite a business being done in Canada in private aircraft, and that quite a number of Canadians were being put at an extreme disadvantage whether they were flying for pleasure or not. I suggest the minister found another problem which he did not tell us about in his speech, that is, not only was it the adverse economic effects and the minimum contribution to conservation, but also the government was having trouble with collections and the enforcement of collection of some of those taxes. There is nothing like tax avoidance to make the government realize that perhaps it was not a good idea to have such a tax in the first place.
We all applauded the reduction in the general sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent. I noticed with interest that the tax is referred to in several places in the bill as a consumption tax. Every time the subject of consumption tax has come up in various debates, it is interesting the government was always quick to point out that consumption taxes are regressive ones which should not be used. The government pointed out that they are hidden taxes, that they weigh hardest on people in the lowest income brackets, and that somehow they are wicked, regressive, and should be avoided.
Everyone realizes that there is retail sales tax on every purchase made in Canada. It is the tax everyone can see when he makes purchases. It is only when the government is making a change in a tax such as this, and when this kind of debate takes place, that Canadian consumers realize the 9 per cent consumption tax is included in the retail price before they pay the retail tax.
Even though the government says that consumption taxes are not very good because they are hidden, it is fair for us to note that every once in a while this government does not mind collecting hidden taxes, which in this case were 12 per cent
March 22, 1979

and are now 9 per cent. If things are collated we know what kind of effect this hidden tax has on the tax of everything we buy. We expected when this tax was reduced to 9 per cent that there would be some sort of reduction in the rate of inflation or the rate of increase in the prices of goods that we buy.
Of course no consideration was given to the inventories on hand when this reduction was introduced. There were countless millions and billions of dollars in inventory around the country on which the tax had already been paid, because the nature of the tax is such that it is paid at the manufacturing level. This inventory had to be sold, and there was no immediate reduction for those business people who had old stock. This had the effect of delaying the benefit to consumers until that inventory was used up.
I hope there is some evidence of a slight reduction in the cost of goods which consumers buy, but I have not heard anybody exclaiming, "Oh, isn't that nice, this item is 3 per cent less than what it cost when I bought it a week ago or a month ago." Certainly there has been no evidence from the monthly bulletins put out by StatsCanada that there has been a reduction in the rate increase in the price of goods. 1 hope that we will see something along this line soon.
There is another aspect of the consumption tax which I wanted to mention briefly. It is an aspect which the government applies through the Income Tax Act, and it does not look upon it as a consumption tax. I am referring to the Registered Retirement Savings Plan I know that we are not debating the Income Tax Act, but I would like to make a comparison between what the government calls an income tax and what is actually a consumption tax.
If a taxpayer in Canada finds that he does not need to spend all of his disposable income in the year in which he receives it, he may contribute it to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan. Within the limits set out in the plan, the taxpayers' contributions are deductible when calculating his or her income tax for that year. The amount which is contributed to the RRSP, together with the interest, is exempt from tax during the time it is a registered plan. When the taxpayer reaches the age of 71 the plan must be deregistered, or it may be done earlier should the taxpayer decide that he needs the money for consumption purposes. When his or her contributions are taken out of the plan, for the purposes of income tax it is considered income for the year in which the plan is collapsed.
Because this plan is covered by the Income Tax Act, the government looks upon it as an income tax. I suggest, however, that in fact this is simply another kind of consumption tax because a consumption tax is levied at the time the item, whatever it may be, is being consumed. Therefore, if this money is taxed when the taxpayer decides that he needs the money for consumption purposes, I suggest that it is in fact a consumption tax, regardless of what the government would like to call it.
There is a very dangerous aspect to this Bill C-38. It is a reference which I have found in several places, and particularly in some of the motions shown in the budget papers. Of course, those motions have been inserted in the bill, but I think
Excise Tax Act
it is easier to find them in the budget papers. For instance, motion No. 5 reads:
The said act be amended to specify the time period within which any amount owing to Her Majesty ... shall be payable-
Motion No. 15 reads:
Subsection 31(2) of the said act be amended to provide that the governor in council, on the joint recommendation of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue-
Suffice it to say, Mr. Speaker, that there are several such examples in the motions. As a matter of fact, here is another one. Motion No. 7 reads:
Authority ... for the Minister of National Revenue to pay such persons as the governor in council may by regulation prescribe-
What we are finding again is more government legislation by regulation rather than by an act of this parliament. I cannot recall the numbers, but it seems to me that in 1978 there were well over 3,000 orders in council issued by the government. Those orders have the same effect as legislation, but they are not subject to the scrutiny of the Elouse or the other place. Such legislation, which gives to the cabinet, the government and the governor in council, the powers contained in it, may be used by the government any number of times and may' have far-reaching effects on the taxpayers and the people of Canada. It is a very serious trend.
During the same period that the Government of Canada was passing, I believe, 3,360 orders in council, the government of Great Britain for the same period passed less than 24 orders in council, and they have the courtesy to ratify their orders later by bringing them into the House.
Bill C-38 is not a very big bill. It seeks only to put into legislation about a page of the minister's budget speech. Yet there are at least three instances where the governor in council is authorized to make regulations over which we, the members who are debating the passing of this bill, will have no say.
I have heard this argument put forth in this House for all the years in which I have been here. It is a situation that is getting worse, not better. More and more power is being taken away from this House in this way and through other means. We no longer find, for instance, that the major announcements are made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the House. The Prime Minister usually decides that other fora are more suitable for his purposes. In fact yesterday we were treated to the first speech by the Prime Minister in this House for five months. The Prime Minister is expected to be just that, the Prime Minister, and to give this House the benefit of his views.
I suppose in the past there has been some justification for the Prime Minister going elsewhere because he might think his message would be more readily disseminated. For the last year and one half, since the introduction of live television broadcasting of the proceedings, and especially in the last two weeks or so when they have been broadcast across the country by satellite, there could be no excuse for him further deteriorating the powers of this House by making major announcements outside it. I am getting a little off the topic, Mr. Speaker, but

March 22, 1979
Excise Tax Act
when I think about what legislation like this is doing to the powers of the House, I have to reflect on what is happening through other forms of erosion.
I have covered the areas I wanted to comment on briefly before the bill goes to committee. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) covered the matter of the increase in the air transportation tax on passenger travel. I hope a serious examination of the effects of the reduction of the sales tax will be made in committee to see whether changes can be made. I hope there will also be close examination of the ever-increasing powers granted to the governor in council by legislation such as this which leaves many important decisions outside the legislation and in the hands of a small group of Canadians, through order in council, decisions which will have an effect on all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the other speakers on this bill. They have had very little to say. I have very little to say either, but since that has not deterred them it will not deter me and I shall make my few remarks.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) addressed some of the broader issues of sales tax and commodity taxes. I know he is partly motivated in that by the responsibilities he shares with me on the finance committee and the time he spent in the last session looking into the question of commodity tax reform. He made the observation, with which no one can argue, that the commodity taxes are hidden taxes and inflationary taxes, in the sense that they make prices higher than they would otherwise be. The other side of that coin is that without the commodity tax system in Canada, income taxes would have to be raised by something like 28 per cent to produce the same amount of revenue for the government. That would have an effect not necessarily as directly inflationary but in its own way it would be an unacceptable alternative. Although it is inflationary it seems to be an unavoidable tax and one that cannot be readily converted to extra points in the Income Tax Act.
I was very happy to see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was able to reduce the sales tax by 3 per cent in this bill, a substantial reduction, which had some immediate impact on retails prices. We know that the over-all impact of a reduction of federal sales tax does not show as readily as a reduction in the retail sales tax which is added to the price of goods at the consumer level. It is obvious that in a competitive market the reduction in the federal sales tax will have some impact on prices. Indeed, the consumer price index reports in the months following the introduction of this measure showed a considerable impact. Some of the movement of prices in the months following this tax change, which have been lower than they would otherwise be, was indicated by Statistics Canada and other sources to be attributable in part to the reduction of the federal sales tax.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra expressed some regret about the length of time it takes for this parliament to

deal with budget legislation. I want to second that. I agree it is regrettable that it takes so long to put budget bills through. It is true they begin to take effect on budget night, but unfortunately certain sectors in the community, private citizens and corporations, are reluctant to act on resolutions that have not become legislation approved by parliament. This problem has become particularly acute since the Department of National Revenue began to increase the amount of assistance offered to taxpayers in the way of interpretation of the impact of legislation and proposed transactions on taxpayers.
Proposals were recently approved by parliament which permit taxpayers to present a proposed transaction to officials of the Department of National Revenue and receive some sort of ruling for their comfort in entering into the proposed transaction. When a budget like this comes along offering many good things to stimulate economic growth, taxpayers have sought the guidance of a ruling from the Department of National Revenue but have found that the department is not in a position to give them the comfort letter or ruling on a proposed transaction until the legislation is passed.
In my constituency a company wanted to buy equipment to do research and development work so that it could take advantage of the incresed incentives offered. It asked the Department of National Revenue for a ruling and was told, quite rightly, that the department does not rule on resolutions, only on legislation. Officials of the department cannot take it for granted that this bill will be passed.
Another case was referred to me today by a chartered accountant. His client proposed to purchase some Dome Petroleum warrants or participation shares in the Beaufort Sea project. These interests were made very attractive under the budget bills, and taxpayers interested in taking advantage of them are entitled to some assurance that when they put their money on the table the promised tax credits will be forthcoming. The Department of National Revenue can give no such assurance until the House deals with these budget bills.
I should like to see more respect on all sides of the House for the impact this problem has on corporations and individuals. It is certainly not a government responsibility to get legislation out of the House; it is a government responsibility to bring legislation into the House. Any member of the House of any party can claim responsibility or be given responsibility for failure to get the legislation out.
I have been urging that a method be found for bringing budget bill legislation to a head, because all parties agree that economic uncertainty is present in the Canadian economy. On this side of the House we feel that the economic uncertainty that exists is not totally justified. The performance of the economy has been good and businessmen are entitled to have a justifiable measure of confidence. The incentives that are offered in this bill do not have their fullest impact until the measures become law, and who knows when that will be?
There are rumours that there may be an election in the weeks or months ahead. If these budget bills do not become

law before the election, will they become law after the election? I say the government will be returned and its commitment to this legislation will continue. One cannot blame a businessman ready to put his money on the table for wanting the certainty of an act of legislation to rely on so that he can invest with certainty and apply to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) and to his officials for the kind of ruling that this government has recently begun to make available to taxpayers with very good effect.
Let me turn to some other provisions. I have already referred to the welcome reduction in the sales tax from 12 per cent to nine per cent. This is very far from the kind of reform that the government has under consideration for the commodity tax of Canada.
The finance committee, which I referred to earlier, has already spent some time in the past session looking at the fundamental problems that exist with the excise and sales taxes in Canada. In particular we have looked at the arbitrariness of the present sales tax act which is 56 years old. It has none of the kinds of provisions such as rights of appeal, rights of review or of statutory determinations which exist in more contemporary legislation. I know all members of this House would welcome legislation to update the Sales Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act. They may remain inflationary, as the hon. member indicates, but they can be much fairer and clearer than they are. They can be designed in a way to be much more helpful and stimulatory to the taxpayers of this country, in their operations in the economy.
I urge the House to deal rapidly with this legislation and to try to get as many of the budget bills enacted as possible. None of us in this House-however much we might try to exploit the existing atmosphere of uncertainty in some parts of this country-want that atmosphere to be perpetuated by the activities of members of parliament and by political partisanship.
I close my remarks by urging members of parliament to come to terms with this important bill. I ask them to try, if possible, in the weeks ahead to pass it, to deliver it into the hands of the economic community, and to deliver to the Minister of National Revenue the means to begin to issue definitive comfort letters and rulings to interested participants in the economic life of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this debate on Bill C-38 and to have the opportunity to give a critique and an analysis of this particular legislation which is now before us. I hear government members applauding the bill. It is quite normal for them to want to support their own piece of legislation, but I want to say that it is the role of the opposition to define, in the concept of the British parliament, and to give a critique of that legislation. My role tonight is to point out some of the specific weaknesses in the bill and if the government wishes it can as a result, make some amendments, and improve the bill.
I wish to comment on a remark made by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) who just preceded me. I may
Excise Tax Act
not be quoting him directly but I believe he said that the commodity taxes are hidden taxes and are inflationary. He went on to rationalize that that was okay. By what I believe is very close to a direct quote he said that if they were removed, income tax would have to be increased by 28 per cent. 1 have never heard of a response so shallow as that particular response. If we follow the reasoning given by the hon. member for York Centre, we can ask the question, where will the line be drawn on taxation? I now cite some figures in this respect.
In 1960, in terms of revenue as a percentage of the gross national product, all governments in Canada took 25.1 per cent. In 1968 that figure had increased to 34.4 per cent, and by 1974, at the start of the thirtieth parliament, the figure had risen to 39.8 per cent. I will now turn to expenditures. In 1950 22.1 per cent of the GNP was spent by governments. By 1968 when this government first took power 33.7 per cent was being spent of our total GNP by all governments in terms of taxation, and by 1974 the figure was 37.9 per cent. As recently as 1977 the figure was 41.1 per cent.
Consider a pie of a certain size. If one continues to increase the percentage that government takes from that pie, that much less money is left for the private sector. In other words, the larger the percentage of gross national product that comes from government expenditures, less is left for the private sector.
The hon. member for York Centre says revenues were needed so certain taxes were added on. I fail to understand this thinking. It would seem more logical for the government to stop and consider how it could bring stimulus into the economy so as to get the free enterprise system working. This would eliminate the need for a heavy overburden of government increasing taxes and working toward the objective of a dominated government society, which we appear to be working toward in Canada today.
Let me take a look at some of the specifics in this bill which do just that. For instance, airport tax has increased from $8 to $15 per person. In the first place Canada is probably one of the last nations in the world-next only to the Soviet Union- that should discourage air traffic. Canada is a country with a large land mass. It has tremendous resources, some of which are found in places where roads, railways and boats cannot go. To discourage aircraft travel, whether by light plane or commercial aircraft, is demonstrating a disincentive to the construction and the building of this country. However, if we were talking about a country such as Belgium which is a small country with a dense population, and if for some reason because of air traffic density the government in its wisdom said that air traffic should be limited, this would be quite proper. But to limit air traffic in Canada by taxation policies does not seem appropriate.
We could extend beyond the particular part of the clause in Bill C-38 and talk about the whole excise tax area and bringing light aircraft into Canada. The whole discriminatory concept against air travel has as its bottom line that this government does not believe that the airplane services the free enterprise system of our country. We have an unimaginative

March 22, 1979
Excise Tax Act
government. Otherwise, we would open up the concept of air travel, making it freer to travel.
On one hand we have an opinion that has been expressed in this House, one in which I concur, by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) that Canadians should travel and tour more in Canada. That is an opinion to which most Canadians would subscribe. However, we cannot take that position and on the other hand put in the way economic roadblocks which have objectives exactly opposite to that. I find it hard to believe that the government thought it necessary to increase the airport tax on the travelling public from $8 to $15. This is one of the last nations in the world that should put roadblocks in the way of air travel.
I now move to another portion of the bill, the reduction of sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent. On the surface that tends to sound very musical to the ears of most people. However, the Department of Finance, which ought to be schooled in economics and the ramifications of their recommendations, should know that when they make a recommendation to reduce sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent, somewhere they catch businessmen in the middle of the year. Car dealers across Canada would love to have this election come for no other reason than to vote against this government on that particular clause. I will tell you why.
A car dealer in my constituency managed to get out of that situation into which the government had put him. He had some cars on the lot at 12 per cent sales tax and others, the same kind of cars, at the 9 per cent sales tax. In order to get out of that, it cost him $12,000 out of his pocket. That is what he spent to bail out this government for not having foresight in terms of a taxation policy.
When you do not make the sales tax retroactive to a fiscal year, all you do is box in those people dealing in major commodity items. They have to pay out of their pockets in order to bail out the government. If the government is going to reduce sales tax, it should give some kind of warning, and the various sectors of the industry will applaud that. It would be widely accepted across the country. However, when you come in with the axe because an election is coming soon and you want some goodies in the candy bag to hand out, and you reduce the sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent, the result is that the private citizen has to bail out the country.
Another part of this tax that leaves us in a real quandary as to what direction the government has been taking is in relation to building materials. In this country we have a shortage of housing and one of the highest levels of unemployment of any of the industrialized nations in the world, except for Italy. We must recognize that many factors flow out of the field of housing. First, it stimulates a tremendous number of sectors of our economy such as the lumber industry, concrete industry, electrical wiring, plumbing, skilled, unskilled and professional people.
The government somehow leaves on the books the concept of having a 5 per cent building tax. Some years ago the tax was

12 per cent. It was dropped a little bit, then some more, and now finally it will be 5 per cent. A bureaucracy is always needed to look after this. Throughout the building materials industry there is extra paperwork. There is just as much paperwork with a one per cent tax as a 90 per cent tax, and just as much administration required for a 5 per cent tax as a 75 per cent tax.
If the government wants to pare some of the administration and take off some of the overburden in the business community, the best thing it could have done would have been to wipe out in total the tax on building materials. It would have given a stimulus to the housing industry. That is the kind of imagination this country needs. It is something that should have been looked at in the last budget.
There is an appalling conflict of position in Bill C-38. It talks of a reduction in tax in terms of solar heaters. It is a good idea and no one in this House would argue with it. However, it slaps a tax on double-glazed window glass and storm doors. Somehow in the political ramifications the government gives the impression it wants to move toward energy saving devices. It picks something that has a musical ring to the public and says it will remove the tax on solar heating. While the public is looking in that direction, it sneaks behind and slaps a tax on storm doors and windows. Are ministers serious about energy saving or not? If they were, they would look at it from a broad perspective and not go on this teeter-totter adventure by taking it off with one hand and putting it on with the other. While Peter is giving, Peter is also taking, and Paul does not know if he is on a Ferris wheel or a pogo stick.
One of the most important parts of this legislation is also one of the greatest frustrations I can express about virtually every piece of legislation brought forward by this government. Clauses 15, 16 and 17 of the bill contain regulatory changes that can be changed by order in council.
I notice it is very close to ten o'clock. Perhaps in one sentence I might point out that in 1978 this country, through the federal government, had 3,970 orders in council. Not a single one was referred back to parliament. By contrast, there were about 15 orders in council in Great Britain and every single one was referred back to parliament. What we end up with is government by regulation, in other words, another attempt to thwart the parliamentary system. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
