subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REDUCED INSURANCE PREMIUMS FOR NON-SMOKERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
HEALTH AND WELFARE-REDUCED INSURANCE PREMIUMS FOR NON-SMOKERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this week I raised a question in the House asking what the government had done or would do to encourage the Canadian insurance industry to offer discounts or premiums to nonsmokers who were physically fit. The answer I received was unsatisfactory because, as I learned later, my question was addressed to the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) whereas it should have been addressed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
Recently I received a substantial discount on my automobile insurance premium because I had not been involved in any kind of car accident for more than five years. Included in my premium notice was a reminder to all those who totally abstain from alcoholic beverages. This group of drivers is also a low risk group and, in consequence, they receive a significant reduction in their premiums. So the principle is well-known in the insurance industry: low risk groups get a break in their insurance costs. Safe drivers and non-drinkers of alcohol are among those in low risk groups.
However, according to a study done in the U.S.A. by a company known as Farmers' Insurance, non-smoking drivers have an accident rate which is one half that of smokers. It is not difficult to understand why smokers who drive may have more accidents; the act of lighting a cigarette, cigar or pipe can be distracting, as can the butting of smoking materials or the brushing away of ashes from clothes and car cushions. On the basis of this study, the Farmers' Insurance Company in the U.S.A. decided to give non-smokers a good discount on premiums. Mr. Speaker, if proper surveys were carried out by the Insurance Bureau of Canada I am sure it would be found that non-smokers are safer and better drivers and should therefore be rewarded by having to pay less for their premiums.
So far, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken only of automobile insurance premiums. But the same principle applies to life insurance. The Occidental Life Insurance Company in the U.S.A. is offering discounts of between 10 per cent and 20 per cent on life insurance premiums to policyholders who exercise regularly. I am advised that, to qualify, a person must sign a statement that he or she is a non-smoker and has done some form of aerobic exercise such as jogging or swimming for a least 20 minutes three days a week for the preceding year. To the best of my knowledge, these progressive measures being followed by some insurance companies in the United States have not been adopted in Canada.
The Government of Canada knows that smoking is a serious threat to health and that it interferes in varying degrees with normal daily activities. Again, the government actively promotes and encourages citizens to follow a regular exercise program. Participaction has contributed a great deal, in my view, to raising the average level of robust good health in Canada. Now is the time to go for additional pay-offs, additional, that is, to feeling better, working more effectively and enjoying life more. The extra pay-off should be applied to
Adjournment Debate
insurance costs. Low risk groups should have their premiums reduced, and what better opportunity is there than on the basis of the evidence which has been produced as a result of studies in the United States?
That is the background for my question. I wanted to know what the minister has done to convince the insurance industry in Canada that this is a logical course to follow. What will the minister do in this regard? Non-smokers are now a majority in this country and it is about time they stopped having to pay extra premiums which have been incurred by those who are smokers.

speakeroldname: Miss Aideen Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REDUCED INSURANCE PREMIUMS FOR NON-SMOKERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity to respond to the hon. member's question. It is not often that we non-smokers see questions raised in this way.
About two years ago an official of the Department of National Health and Welfare raised with the Canadian Home Office Life Insurance Underwriters Association the possibility of offering a reduced premium to their non-smoking clients. At that time it was pointed out that non-smokers make up approximately 70 per cent of the total population of Canada. Shortly afterwards one Canadian company offered a reduced rate on fire insurance, which is between 20 per cent and 25 per cent less than the standard premium. The same company also provides automobile insurance at a rate which is about 15 per cent less than the standard premium. No other Canadian company offers these reduced rates.
The question of reduced life insurance rates for Canadian non-smokers has also been explored with the industry. Canadian statistics on morbidity and mortality, as well as United States statistics, particularly those used by at least one American insurance company, seem to indicate that non-smokers are good risks and that it might be logical to offer them a preferred rate. This has not yet happened in Canada, although departmental officials continue to discuss the matter with the industry with the aim of obtaining the same life insurance benefits for Canadian non-smokers as those enjoyed by our American neighbours south of the border.
One can hope that the competitive requirements of the insurance industry will eventually produce the kind of premium reduction suggested by the hon. member.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-AUTHORITY OF CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD TO PURCHASE GRAIN HOPPER CARS
TRANSPORT-AUTHORITY OF CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD TO PURCHASE GRAIN HOPPER CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a non-smoker I also endorse the physical fitness concepts of my good friends opposite. I am looking forward to the conclusion of this parliament so that I can start jogging.
My question deals with a question I asked on February 12, 1979, of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), after the Canadian Wheat Board purchased some 2,000 hopper cars using Canadian Wheat Board or, in essence, farmers' money.

March 22, 1979
Adjournment Debate
The question was whether there was any limit to the number of hopper cars the board could buy, and the minister said that because there is authority, of course there was not. Then I went on to ask him if there was therefore any reason why the Canadian Wheat Board could not also purchase engines to pull trains, repair tracks on which grain is hauled, and repair terminals, ports and the like. The minister's response to me was as follows:
The answer to that question is no, Mr. Speaker; and, of course, it is completely out of the context of any reality to put it, except perhaps to create worry.
The minister went on to say:
They may save as much in demurrage charges at that time or in the ability to make spot sales in the annual cost of these cars, and that is the reasoning they employed.
I was not satisfied with that answer because I did not believe it. Today the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk) put virtually the same question, and he received a very different and conflicting answer. Today the minister said that the board has its own authority on this matter. 1 am referring to the "blues" of this afternoon's question period. The minister said that the Canadian Wheat Board went back and concluded that the right thing to do would be to go ahead and make purchases. I wrote a letter to the minister to ask about this, and I will quote a paragraph of the letter I wrote to the minister, as follows:
So that I might be precisely informed as to the specific authority that grants the Canadian Wheat Board the power to make the above said purchases, I would be pleased if you would cite the regulations or statutes that grant the Canadian Wheat Board the right to take such action.
I have now received a response which reads in part:
In reply to your letter of February 12, 1979 regarding Canadian Wheat Board authority to purchase hopper cars, this authority is contained in section 4 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, Chapter 12, as amended.
The following paragraphs of section 4.4 are the pertinent to this matter: Paragraph (a) empowers the board "to buy, take delivery of, store, transfer,
sell, ship or otherwise dispose of grain"-
The fact is that they could buy the engines and build the railway lines, and build anything else in accordance with the wishes of the Canadian Wheat Board to enable them to sell, ship or otherwise dispose of grain. This provides me with a very interesting perspective in view of the fact that a week ago I met with the president and executive of CP Rail who stated that CP is no longer sure they can pay $800,000 per rail engine, and that grain trains often use as many as four of these $800,000 engines.
The fundamental question is not with regard to the 2,000 hopper cars. What I would like to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lapointe) tonight is this: we want some assurance, as we go through the list in this letter, a portion of which I read, stating that since they purchased 2,000 hopper cars and that the Canadian Wheat Board says it would like to have 10,000 hopper cars, they can no longer give an assurance that they can afford to purchase the engines, and noting the fact that some railway lines handle nothing but grain, what guarantee can he give to the farming

community that after they have seeded the grain, fertilized it, used pesticides and herbicides, then harvested it, stored it and hauled it to the grain elevators, the Canadian Wheat Board will not use up all their money to improve the transport system without paying the farmers?
I should like to quote a section of the Revised Statutes of Canada relating to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The pertinent paragraph in the minister's reply reads as follows:
Paragraph (d) empowers the board "to acquire, hold and dispose of real and personal property ..Legal officers consulted were unanimously of the opinion that personal property includes such items as hopper cars.
Why could it not include any other item? It was their decision that it included hopper cars. In his answer to me the minister said that obviously they could not purchase the engines or fix up the rail beds or the ports. I do not believe that answer because of the different answer he gave today to the hon. member for Portage in which he indicated that the Canadian Wheat Board can use its money in any way it deems fit so long as it is for the purpose of buying, selling, shipping or otherwise disposing of grain. This is the first time in Canadian history that the Canadian Wheat Board has used farmers' money for any other purpose than to pay demurrage charges which occur on the west coast usually because of strikes or because of the unfortunate scheduling of ships coming to port.
We are now on the threshold of a change in how farmers' dollars are used. What I would like to know from the parliamentary secretary this evening is what assurances he can give us, clearly and simply, that the farmers from this day henceforth, when they make a sale of grain, will get even $1 back, and that somehow in the judgment of the Canadian Wheat Board it will not be necessary to use that money to fix up some rail lines or to buy some more hopper cars or engines to pull the grain, or to fix up the grain drying facilities, or a whole host of other expenses. If that act is to be interpreted in the loose way it is drafted, it cannot be left simply to the judgment of the elected officials of the Canadian Wheat Board. There must be a distinct difference between making policy direction decisions and decisions which relate to the actual dollars that go back to the farmers' pockets. I should like the parliamentary secretary to address himself to that second point.

March 22, 1979

What surprises me even more, Mr. Speaker, is that if the hon. member had indeed listened to the answers the minister gave today the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk) he would probably not have to quote from the letters he wrote or even the statutes of Canada.
May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to quote in turn, the way the hon. member did, the answer the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) gave today to the question by the hon. member for Portage, on exactly the same subject when the minister indicated with respect to the purchase of 2,000 hopper cars by the Canadian Wheat Board, and I quote:

-indicated at that time that my consent was not required and that the board had its own authority in this matter. I had advance knowledge of its consideration of the matter, and of course I realized they had discussed the matter with the elected advisory committee of producers. After public reaction about the hopper cars, I was concerned that they review the matter.
The minister went on to say that the Wheat Board went back to the advisory committee, looked at it again, and concluded again that the right thing was to go ahead with the purchase.

With respect to the second point, Mr. Speaker, about farmers and the funds necessary to operate the Canadian Wheat Board, the minister clearly indicated they too have a word to say in the decisions of the Canadian Wheat Board, and I would like to quote from the answer the minister gave in this House today as follows:

-that there is an elected body of advisers to the Wheat Board who were elected just freshly toward the end of last year, the first year of their term." They were consulted, but beyond that, as tc what they can or cannot do in precise legal terms, the minister suggested that the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk) should consult his own advisers.
The decision of the Canadian Wheat Board must be taken in the context of what the federal government has accomplished over the past few years to upgrade the grain handling and transportation system. The government has already purchased 8,000 hopper cars for grain movement at the cost of $260 million.

Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the government constantly reassesses the need to purchase additional hopper cars. However, it must make sure these are absolutely necessary before allocating public funds for that purpose. That precaution is particularly important in this period of government restrictions.
To get the most out of the cars used for hauling grain, Mr. Speaker, we see that improved efficiency in the past three years shows one third fewer cars were required in 1977 to haul the same amount of grain as was moved in 1974.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-STEPS TO IMPROVE CAPE BRETON COAL INDUSTRY
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-STEPS TO IMPROVE CAPE BRETON COAL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister, in his answers to my questions of March 15, for giving the people of Cape Breton such hope, and especially for assuring coal miners and the unemployed that they could expect a positive answer from the federal government on the question of opening a new coal mine at Donkin outside the town of Glace Bay.
The minister mentioned that the past help given to the coal division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation is a sign that the Cape Breton mining communities can anticipate good news about Donkin. That is how I interpreted his answer to my supplementary question. I want to tell him we all appreciate that help. Despite some mistakes, Devco's coal division has done a better job for the miners than its predecessors, Dosco and Hawker-Siddeley, which fed at the federal government from the 1920s until they abandoned Cape Breton in the mid-1960s.
In passing I just want the minister to know that if the Liberal government has listened to the late MP, Mr. Clary Gillis, in 1947, it would have nationalized the mines in Cape Breton earlier. If it had adopted his plea for a national fuels policy then we all would have been better off in Canada and we would not have had to wait until the end of the 1970s to get some adequate measures with regard to coal reserves in Cape Breton.
The drilling measures carried on in the last two years have been very encouraging. In the words of the late Devco president, Mr. Bob Matheson, "The coal that was drilled in front of Lingan and No. 26 indicates that Lingan, instead of having a lifespan of 17 years, probably will be able to continue viably for 25 years and this automatically extends the life expectancy of No. 26 as well because it is on the same front."
A paper written by Mr. W. Potter, geologist, on the results of the offshore coal drilling program of 1978, had this to say in paragraph two: "Three holes were drilled at Donkin to examine the quality of the coal found during the 1977 program and to assist the feasibility study for a proposed new mine. The geological resources for the four seams, that is Point Aconi, Lloyd Cove, Hub and Harbour, are two billion tons." Reserves were also found that hopefully will see a new mine at the Prince mine site on the north side.
We all realize that having such a large amount of coal does not mean that present mining technology or the economics of extracting the coal are all favourable. Certainly the coal has been proven to be of good quality for thermal use, if not for coke oven use in a steel plant. Therefore the demand of the Nova Scotia government and its power commission play a crucial role in determining the beginning date for the tunneling operation that must procede the actual extraction of the coal. There is every indication from the premier of Nova

March 22, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Scotia and his minister of mines that they are anxious to get the Donkin mine started as soon as possible.
The minister of mines, Mr. Barkhouse, who is also chairman of the Nova Scotia energy council, sent a telegram to the minister in charge of Devco, Mr. Lessard, on February 27, which in essence urges the federal government to open Donkin. This is good news but before a final announcement of a starting date for opening Donkin can be given, the contractual price demanded by the Nova Scotia Power Commission, as well as royalty rates and length of contracts, all have to be negotiated between Devco and the Nova Scotia Power Commission. The present royalty paid to Nova Scotia government is 25 cents per ton. Is that going to be constant for the life of the Donkin contract?
When does the province intend to build the third and fourth stages of the generating station at Lingan? The first two stages which will produce 300 megawatts of electricity at a cost of some $180 million are due on stream by 1980. They will burn some 800,000 tons of coal. The next two stages or, if there is only a third stage, will produce an additional 300 megawatts and burn another 800,000 tons.
The accelerating price of crude and bunker C oil, which all the evidence shows will go much higher, is a special incentive to use coal-fired thermal plants. Given the insecurity of foreign oil supplies, security of supply from having coal at the backdoor, so to speak, is another very important reason for going ahead without further delay. It will take some four to six years to develop a mine producing some two million tons a year from Donkin. The federal promise of last year should now be confirmed, and Devco and the Nova Scotia government should start negotiating immediately.
There is no good reason that I can see why the Donkin mine cannot be started by June or July. There is every indication that this will prove to be a good investment for the federal government and the Nova Scotia government, as we try to limit imports of foreign oil. Millions and millions of dollars of oil compensation payments by the federal government will be saved. Our country's serious balance of payments situation will be helped. The desperate unemployment problem in the construction and in the coal mining sector of Cape Breton will be greatly alleviated. These are the major important economic and social benefits that will far outweigh financial costs involved.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-STEPS TO IMPROVE CAPE BRETON COAL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words about Devco tonight. I am sure that the hon.
member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) shares my pride and that of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) in the solid record of achievement of Devco.
Devco is an excellent example of the courage and determination of Cape Bretoners and what they can achieve when backed by a committed federal government. It should be widely recognized and appreciated that Devco has turned the Cape Breton coal industry around, that, for example, the Lingan mine is recognized by mining experts around the world as the most productive advancing longwall coal mine in the world.
The hon. member has raised the question of the proposed new Donkin mine. Let there be no doubt as to this government's commitment to do everything possible to develop a viable mine near Donkin. It was this government that spent over $10 million to finance the coal exploration which proved the reserves necessary to support a new mine. It is this government, through Devco, that is paying for the feasibility study of which the hon. member speaks. It is this government that committed itself in principle almost a year ago to proceed with a new Donkin mine if it is shown to be feasible.
The engineering consulting firm which Devco engaged to do the feasibility study on the Donkin mine proposal is now in the final stages of writing its report to the corporation. The report will be a rather lengthy document of up to six volumes, and as soon as it is ready the corporation will make a copy available to the minister and review the document with him.
One volume of the report will be an executive summary and this volume will be the first released. The hon. member may be assured that we shall keep him advised of the progress of this matter.
The hon. member expressed concern as to whether or not the final federal decision will be made before, during or after the election campaign. This is a most difficult question to judge. As the hon. member knows, there is much work involved in evaluating a report of this size. He knows as well that no technical report can replace good policy judgment even though those reports are an essential part of decision making. He knows too that Devco must prepare its plan for development for government approval.
I can only assure him that the government will move with the same determination it has demonstrated in the past and that a decision will be made as quickly as possible.
